speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NATO-DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT OF FRANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and ask whether the government has recently received representations from the government of France, or from General de Gaulle, relating to a new form or direction for the NATO alliance. I ask the question because of an article in today's issue of Le Devoir reporting an alleged statement made by Mr. Pompidou, the French premier, that in line with recent events in the Soviet union and China, NATO's strategic concept must be completely revamped. Has the Canadian government had any discussions in this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NATO-DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT OF FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman has raised a matter of considerable importance. There have been no direct communications from the government of France on this subject, but the attitude the government of France takes toward the military organization of NATO has been the subject of considerable discussion between Canada and France and between the government of France and the other members of NATO.
The publicly stated position of the president of France was referred to by the French foreign minister two days ago in the statement made with regard to the m.l.f. and its relation to NATO. I may say that one of the reasons I asked Mr. Paul-Henri Spaak, the foreign minister of Belgium, to come to Ottawa was in regard to this problem. Today I am having discussions with Mr. Lange, the foreign minister of Norway. Our discussions will have to do with some aspects of this situation.
I would simply like to say that NATO represents for Canada a very essential element of our foreign and military policy. We regard the participation of France in NATO as one of
the most important components in the integrity and unity of that organization. We hope there will be no development on the part of any member of the organization that would in any way result in less interest in NATO or a withdrawal from it. I can assure my right hon. friend this whole question is being carefully examined.

subtopic: NATO-DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT OF FRANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the minister on the necessity of maintaining a strong and effective NATO organization and not permitting the cement which joins the various nations to become weakened in any way. However, the minister made a statement, referring to the attitude that France is taking toward NATO, that I think should be amplified. What are the implications of that statement? Does it in any way convey a decision on the part of France, or a fear that France may separate itself from this organization so necessary to the preservation of western defence?

subtopic: NATO-DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT OF FRANCE
speechtext:
It is well known, Mr. Speaker, that the government of France has taken a position with regard to the integration of forces in NATO. Its view has been stated on many occasions. It is also known that the government of France, through its foreign minister, has recently confirmed its views about m.l.f., the multilateral nuclear force proposal which has been put forward by the United States. Beyond this I cannot go without interfering with discussions which are now under way.
No intimation has been given by the government of France as to the position it would take if its views did not prevail. I expressed the opinion strongly a moment ago, and I confirm it, that it would be a matter of the greatest regret if the government of France were to take any position, or be caused to take any position, which in our judgment would render less strong the integrity of NATO, particularly at this time in world affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that during the months that have passed since last year's estimates were up for consideration by the house in December there have been numerous occasions when defence matters have been discussed in parliament, I wish to preface my remarks today by saying that I will attempt not to duplicate the information already submitted in previous debates.
In addition to the debates in the house, the special committee on defence was re-established in May on this year and has had the opportunity to study many important subjects relating to defence policy generally. On behalf of the government I should like to express our appreciation for the conscientious work of the members of the committee. Certainly the recommendations contained in the report submitted to the house on October 1 have received careful study and consideration by my colleague the associate minister and myself, and by officials of the department.
Debates in the House of Commons include the one on the establishment of the United Nations force in Cyprus in March; the one in May prior to the establishment of the special committee on defence; the one relating to the amendment of the National Defence Act incorporated in Bill No. C-90 in May and later
9838	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence at the end of June; and finally the discussion which followed the acceptance of the motion of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition to adjourn the ordinary business of the house in order to discuss the Cyprus situation on August 10.
In addition, in March parliament and the Canadian people were furnished with a white paper on defence which outlined the defence policy of the present government. Since the purpose of the white paper was to project defence policy into the years ahead, I am sure the committee will agree that this paper should be the basis of the discussions we are now commencing in respect to the estimates of the Department of National Defence for the year 1964-65.
This year, as set out in the blue book, the government is asking for the approval by this committee of estimated expenditures of $1,525,000,000. This figure is a reduction of some $109 million from the estimate of $1,634,000,000 for 1963-64. Of necessity the estimates we are now considering were prepared prior to the completion of the white paper, but they do reflect to a considerable extent the studies which were carried out within the department and which were referred to in my remarks last December.
Hon. members will, I know, be interested in the progress that has been made over the year, and in particular in the steps which have been taken to implement announcement policy. Before going on to this, however, I would like to make a brief reference to the strategic situation now existing.
The real balance of power in the world has not changed materially since the white paper on defence was tabled. There have been developments, however, of some significance. There has been a change in leadership in the Soviet union. Early reports do not indicate any major change in Soviet foreign policy, and there have been what appear to be reassuring statements to this effect. It is too soon to determine for certain, however, that there will be no change in the direction established by the Khrushchev administration, and some time will be required to permit an adequate assessment. During this time of uncertainty it would be prudent for NATO forces to remain alert and for NATO governments to be ready to respond to any genuine gestures offering a prospect of easing world tensions.
Communist China has now succeeded in exploding its first nuclear device, a possibility


which was forecast in the white paper. Although this test came as no particular surprise, it does show that the Chinese have sufficient technical knowledge to permit them to develop a nuclear arsenal. The immediate effect of this explosion is to increase Chinese military prestige so as to overawe their Asian neighbours. It was indicated in the white paper that it will be some years before they would have any substantial long range delivery capability even if they were to divert a consideration proportion of their resources to this end. However, the long term consequences are important and should not be minimized.
An important development during the year was the events which led to conflict on the island of Cyprus, posing as they do a threat to international peace and to the security of the eastern Mediterranean flank of NATO. The circumstances leading to this have been fully dealt with by my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I should like to make reference to the outstanding part played by the Canadian armed forces in implementing the decision taken by the Canadian government and by parliament. I do not wish to repeat what has already been said in the debate in August, but perhaps a brief summary might give some indication of our demonstrated capability.
On the day the Canadian government approved the dispatch to Cyprus Canadian personnel, an advance party of 26 left Trenton. The actual airlifting of troops was started on March 15 and was completed by March 22. H.M.C.S. Bonaventure left Halifax on March 18 and arrived off Cyprus on the 30th, carrying vehicles with their drivers and some 92 tons of cargo. On April 10, in response to a request by the secretary general of the United Nations, some 156 additional personnel were sent to Cyprus to provide a brigade headquarters for the United Nations force. Finally on August 13, again in response to a request from the United Nations, Canada sent an anti-tank platoon.
Over the months that the United Nations force has been in operation in Cyprus, the Canadian element of that force has performed in a manner of which all Canadians can be proud. I was fortunate to be able to visit Cyprus in June, to have had the opportunity to meet at first hand our troops there and to be briefed by Canadian officers in the field on what exactly Canadians were being called upon to do. I was extremely impressed and extremely proud of our men.
The situation in Cyprus has been fraught with difficulty but, as the Secretary of State

for External Affairs has informed the house, within the last few weeks there has been a period of comparative quiet, and I myself believe that the presence of the United Nations force, of which Canadian personnel form a very substantial part, has been one of the most significant factors leading to the improved conditions. Certainly the government, in agreeing to extend Canada's participation for a further three months, put great dependence on this fact. The six month rotation has been completed with the same smoothness and efficiency that was evidenced last March, the whole operation being carried out in nine days.
Conflict, and the possibility of conflict, continues in many parts of the world; in South Viet Nam, on the border between Indonesia and Malaysia, in Cyprus, in Yemen, in the Congo, etc. While Canada is not directly involved in all these areas, they are all areas of concern to us as they affect the peace and stability of the world situation.
I would now like to discuss operational readiness and operational capability. A year ago none of the squadrons of the air division in Europe were operational in the strike and reconnaissance roles undertaken by Canada in 1959. In the intervening months the operational status has changed dramatically. The necessary agreements have been reached to permit the storage of the special ammunition for the strike role, and the six squadrons of CF-104's stationed in Germany are now operational. The two reconnaissance squadrons stationed at Marville in France have undergone intensive operational training for some months and are expected to reach full aircrew establishment in early 1965.
In accordance with the commitment given by the government, decisions have been taken which will permit all aircraft in the air division to have an alternate non-nuclear support role capability. Contrary to one or two articles which have appeared in the newspapers, the modifications required to permit these airplanes to carry conventional armaments are not great. We anticipate that it will be possible to proceed in an orderly fashion to give the aircraft and the aircrews this dual capability.
In the past year the operational capability of the brigade group stationed in Germany has been improved by the addition of 12 Centurion tanks to the armoured regiment and the formation of an anti-tank company which is being issued with a new anti-tank guided missile now being received from contract. Selected personnel from Canada and the brigade group have attended anti-tank guided
Supply-National Defence missile instructor courses, and a missile controller course for operators was conducted in the brigade this summer. Graduates of this course are manning the anti-tank weapon systems of the Royal 22nd regiment company now in Germany.
As hon. members know, the brigade group has included an Honest John artillery battery since early 1962. Until this summer, however, the battery was unarmed. Recently, following the signing of the necessary agreements, the battery has become operational.
For several years it has been obvious that the brigade group suffered one notable deficiency in equipment, that is the absence of armoured personnel carriers. The decision taken last year to acquire the M-113 armoured personnel carrier has resulted in initial deliveries, with production quantities to be available early in the new year. By midsummer the total complement for the brigade group should be available for Europe. The availability of armoured personnel carriers will result in a marked qualitative improvement in the operational capability of the brigade group.

Another important addition will be the provision of a transport helicopter platoon. Following the delivery of heavy transport cargo helicopters now under contract and the training of crews to operational standards, the platoon will be moved to Europe to provide logistic and tactical air mobility.
To increase the fire power of the brigade group, two 105 mm. batteries of artillery are being replaced with two 155 mm. batteries.
To increase the transport capability of the Royal Canadian Air Force the decision was taken some months ago to augment the inventory of C130E Hercules aircraft. An order was placed for 16 C130E Hercules planes and the first of these will be delivered shortly, the balance to follow in the period between now and August of next year. The C130E is a remarkably good aircraft which can operate from unimproved airstrips, and its short landing and take-off characteristics are ideal for the support of the Canadian army in mobile operations.
There has been a steady improvement in the fighting efficiency and modernization of

Supply-National Defence our antisubmarine ships. Two new destroyer escorts have been added to the fleet. H.M.C.S. Nipigon has been commissioned and H.M.C.S. Annapolis will be coming into service in December. These two ships are fitted with both variable depth sonar and full facilities for operating large antisubmarine helicopters. Trials of the Canadian developed "haul down" gear to enable these helicopters to operate effectively in rough weather are proceeding satisfactorily.
Concurrently the conversion of the seven St. Laurent class destroyer escorts has been proceeding. This conversion brings these escorts up to full Nipigon standards. Two ships are already fully converted and back in service and the third, the Ottawa, is about to be recommissioned. H.M.C.S. Assiniboine, the first ship converted, has been making excellent progress in trials operating the latest antisubmarine helicopter, the CHSS-2 Sea King, from her own flight deck and hangar. This combination gives every promise of being completely successful and, if this is so, the combination of operating a destroyer escort with its own antisubmarine helicopter as a single weapons system will increase by several times the effective surveillance which can be furnished by our antisubmarine fleet.
The first of three new submarines of the Oberon class, the Ojibwa, was launched last February, and in June the keel was laid for the second, the Onondaga. The acquisition of these submarines will not only increase our operational capability but will also be invaluable for training purposes.
Development of the hydrofoil as a potential antisubmarine vehicle is continuing. Along with the development of a prototype ocean going craft is the development of its associated weapons system. We wish to determine the feasibility and effectiveness of a high speed hydrofoil antisubmarine vessel in conjunction with other naval forces. The design being developed is based on a concept by the defence research board which is unique and different from those being developed in other countries. The weapons system for the hydrofoil will include variable depth sonar and homing torpedoes. The target date for completion of the construction of the prototype is mid-1966. Any plans for operational use of the hydrofoil will have to await evaluation of the seagoing trials.
It is interesting to note that the British government is concentrating on the development of hovercraft ships in the same role. This will permit concurrent development of two entirely different concepts in the two countries,

with full information in respect of developments being made available to the other. By concentrating its efforts on one of the two concepts each country will be making the best use of its resources, and will at the same time have access to the benefits of new knowledge derived from each. There is a full exchange of technical information in respect of these craft among the United States, Canada and Britain.
Some months ago a study was undertaken in the Department of National Defence to determine the best combination of ships and weapons systems for the antisubmarine role. This study was completed on schedule and is now being studied by the integrated defence staff. We anticipate that it will be possible to take some decisions and indicate our initial requirements for new ships within a few weeks.
Over the past several years Canada has worked in close co-operation with the United States in respect of air defence of the North American continent. The white paper pointed out certain fundamental questions which will have to be answered before it is possible to determine what role will be required in air defence in the years ahead. In particular, the deployment or non-deployment of an antiintercontinental ballistic missile system will have a direct bearing on future plans. Until this major decision is taken there are many questions which must remain unanswered.
In the present strategic situation it is considered worth while to maintain fully operational anti-bomber defences. In this connection Canada has increased, and continues to increase, the capability of its contribution to the anti-bomber defences. The arming of the two Bomarc missile squadrons has doubled the number of vehicles available in this role. We have reduced the number of interceptor squadrons from five to three in order to reduce overhead and increase efficiency, but the acquisition of the MB1G missile expected in the new year will increase the effective operational capability of our interceptor forces by a significant order of magnitude.

Yes. Canada has been playing and will continue to play its full part in the collective security of the North American continent.
In this regard it is perhaps advisable to lay at rest the newspaper speculation that the NORAD agreement would not be renewed. This report was without any foundation whatever. From a strategic standpoint the security

of the North American continent is indivisible; therefore the NORAD agreement, or a similar arrangement, is a continuing requirement. The Canadian government has no intention of withdrawing from full partnership in co-operation with the United States in the collective security of the continent.
As part of our program to increase the operational readiness of our forces and to ensure maximum co-operation both within the services and with our allies, we have participated and will be participating in a number of major exercises. Some examples of these exercises that have been held so far this year are as follows. In February, units of the army and the R.C.A.F. carried out an airborne, air transported exercise to test plans for regional defence operations. In another, the Royal Canadian Navy, R.C.A.F. and army tested the embarkation, transportation and logistic support of a company group of 3 CIBG ready force. The most recent one was Yeoman, in which the 3 CIBG ready force was moved by sea to Argentia, Newfoundland from Saint John, New Brunswick and Halifax, Nova Scotia. H.M.C.S. Provider and nine escorts as well as R.C.A.F. aircraft from air transport command and maritime air command participated along with United States naval personnel stationed at Argentia.
An international exercise was conducted in February and March in an area off Ceylon which included naval forces from Canada and was designed to exercise combined commonwealth forces in the conduct of war operations and to advance standards of efficiency in weapons. Other countries participating in this exercise were Britain, Australia, India, Malaysia and New Zealand. Another exercise in April included units of the R.C.N. and maritime air command along with units from the United States, Britain and the Netherlands to further the development and improve the tactics, doctrine, command and control arrangements for antisubmarine warfare barrier operations. In September, Slamex was an exercise in combined antisubmarine warfare operations to evaluate the effectiveness of available Canadian and U.S. forces in coordinated defensive operations against missile launching submarines off the east coast of this continent.
Joint Canada-U.S. exercises are continually taking place to test the effectiveness of our air defences here, while in Europe both the 4th brigade group and the air division have joined with the land and air forces of our NATO allies in training manoeuvres to ensure their maximum effectiveness.
Supply-National Defence
For the immediate future, further exercises are planned which will provide cold weather winter warfare training at Fort Wainwright and, in conjunction with the United States, units of the army and air transport command will conduct cold weather operations in Alaska. Also, in December an exercise will be held in Newfoundland to gain experience in securing an air force base against ground attack with units from all three services and the U.S.A.F. co-operating. These are only a few of the many national and international exercises in which the armed forces are participating, either here at home, in Europe, or in other areas where conditions are conducive to furthering the capability of the armed forces to be prepared for any eventuality.
I have spoken at some length about our contribution to NATO and to NORAD, since the major part of our defence effort is concentrated in those areas in so far as manpower and expenditures are concerned. However, our military contribution to the United Nations peace forces, as hon. members know, plays an important part in international stability and has a not inconsiderable impact on the defence budget.
Looking in isolation at the various United Nations operations to which Canada makes a contribution does not give a true picture of our involvement in this important area. Quite apart from the Congo, from which the United Nations force was withdrawn this summer and to which Canada supplied an important element of specially trained personnel, at the present time we have 17 Canadian officers forming part of the United Nations truce supervisory organization between Israel on the one hand and the United Arab Republic, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria on the other. Over 800 army personnel and some 100 R.C.A.F. personnel are stationed in the Gaza strip to guard against border violations between Israel and the United Arab Republic. In Cyprus we have about 1,200 Canadians. Twelve Canadian officers and five other ranks form part of the United Nations military observer group whose role is to supervise the terms of the cease fire agreement between India, Pakistan and Kashmir, and some 47 officers and 35 other ranks are part of the international supervisory commissions comprising members from Canada, India and Poland in Laos and Viet Nam.
In so far as the newly independent countries are concerned, Canadian armed forces personnel are providing training assistance to Ghana and Nigeria, while training in Canada is being given to a number of service personnel

Supply-National Defence from other commonwealth countries. Military-survey teams have been sent to Tanganyika
and Malaysia to determine the military training and equipment assistance Canada might appropriately give them, having regard to our other military and financial commitments.
As indicated in the white paper, it was decided that the best method of ensuring the rapid and effective integration of Canada's armed forces would be to start at the top. This is the procedure being followed. Bill C-90, amending the National Defence Act, was passed by parliament after due deliberation and came into effect on August 1, 1964. On that day the positions of Chairman, chiefs of staff committee, and the chiefs of the individual services were abolished and the new organization established. The new organization consists of the chief of the defence staff, the vice chief of defence staff, the assistant chief of defence staff, and four functional chiefs- operational readiness, personnel, logistics and engineering, and comptroller general.
Since the bill was proclaimed the reorganization has been developing stage by stage. The first stage being considered is the complete integration of Canadian forces headquarters. This process has now reached the higher levels and will continue until all the positions required for the new integrated headquarters have been filled. The target figure for savings at Canadian force headquarters is approximately one third throughout all ranks, and will be possible as a result of the formation of an integrated staff and the elimination of duplication and triplication. It is anticipated that the new integrated headquarters will be largely organized on the reduced scale within a year. Some special problems pertaining to the logistics and engineering branch exist, however, and progress in this area in making the planned reductions may not be as rapid as in other branches.
Throughout the integration process new methods are being developed and new policies established. We are attempting to take the best from the several systems previously in operation and to apply them as a whole. In the case of logistics, for example, this will mean extending the automated system presently in use by the air force throughout the three services.
Now that the integration of the Canadian forces headquarters is well under way, preliminary thought is being given to the integration of commands. It is anticipated that within a few months it will be possible to
[Mr. Hellyer.l

evolve a careful long range plan which will permit considerable financial savings while at the same time maintaining and, hopefully, even improving the efficiency of units. Stage three will involve the integration of schools and other facilities. This will follow naturally and logically from stage two. While it is difficult to predict the time cycle required for the whole process, it is anticipated that the major elements of integration can take place, and the most important savings effected, within three years.
The special service force is being formed by modifying an existing Canadian army brigade group to provide a light mobile force smaller than our brigade groups assigned to NATO. The force is to be air transportable, with some of its equipment air droppable. The force will consist of a headquarters and three infantry battalions, light artillery, engineer and signals elements and other ancillary and support units as required to enable the force to carry out its various operational commitments. For instance, a reconnaissance squadron from the newly formed reconnaissance regiment might be assigned to this force. Similarly, if it requires heavier weapons such as tanks or anti-tank guns, these will be provided from our other conventional units. Should the force require an airborne capability, a parachute element will be assigned to it.
A number of major equipment items implicit in the white paper have been under serious study for some time. As I indicated earlier, I hope to be able to announce within a few weeks a substantial part of our shipbuilding program for the next few years. The same applies to aircraft. We have been giving detailed study to our requirements for tactical aircraft in a close ground support role, and it is hoped that a decision can be made in this respect, too, within a reasonable length of time. Also under consideration is the possibility of acquiring self propelled artillery, and reconnaissance and other vehicles for the army.
In summation I would like to say that notwithstanding the reduction in expenditures, we will have achieved within two years a significant qualitative improvement and operational capability of our armed forces. Further qualitative improvements will take place as new equipment becomes available and new tactics are developed. We are at the same time involved in an historic reorganization which will put us in the forefront of developments in the field of military organization.

We fully appreciate the problems that ara inherent in any such reorganization. No improvements can be effected, whether they be the installation of new streets or lights or water systems, without some temporary inconvenience and dislocation. The same problem applies in respect to the integration of our forces. In order to effect permanent and worth-while improvements, temporary inconvenience and dislocation is inevitable. We are deeply grateful for the patient understanding of those who have been affected, and we will do our utmost to minimize the problems that we will create for others during this transitional period.

The minister has referred to the white paper. With the passage of time I have not revised my opinion with respect to the white paper, in that I feel it has been greatly overestimated and there has been a great deal of ballyhoo in regard to it. It has not materially changed from white papers in the past, and I think we have made our views known in this regard. There was a great deal of ballyhoo with regard to estimated savings, or what were thought to be savings or projected savings to be savings, but nowhere is there any concrete evidence as to these savings. I think we will have to depend upon experience to see whether there actually was not a real flim-flam in this regard.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I think it would be instructive to read the last October 7 report of the meeting of the Canadian air industry in Quebec city. The following is attributed to the air chief marshal, who is reported as having said:
-the proposed integrated armed forces will provide savings for defence spending, but a speedy decision was difficult to make while the forces were working out the many problems of intergrating forces management.
Supply-National Defence
He did say that he expects a saving but that this cannot be expected immediately. In the early stages, certainly, one cannot anticipate these savings of which the minister spoke and about which there was the usual publicity surrounding the issuing of this white paper. I am sure the minister, in retrospect, will agree that there was a great deal of optimism but that the actual carrying out or the implementation of some of these plans will indicate that the so-called savings are just not there. I think it was wrong too, to say there would be savings, if it was the minister's intention, as I think it was, to devote the moneys that he could take from one sector for use in another. These are not savings; this is a reallocation of funds and a redirection of spending.
There is no quarrel with the basic principles involved in this; but to talk about savings and say they were going to save perhaps a billion dollars over ten years is a lot of nonsense, unless the minister intends to reduce the role of the armed services. He tackled one portion of the over-all defence expenditures which was nothing new to his advisers; it was information that was available and was being acted on by the previous administration. It is a problem that has occurred not only in this country but in all countries, in that really the housekeeping costs were getting out of line; and not only a little out of line. They were built into the system. The minister has tackled this problem by trying to bring about integration. We will see whether that is going to work out in so far as a saving or a making of funds available for other expenditures is concerned.
I noted the remarks the minister made with regard to the progress of unification of command. I call it unification of command; I do not call it integration, because I do not think it is yet integration. It is purely unification of command. This is a desirable step all the way along. Obviously there are going to be some difficulties in this connection. Again I think a great fanfare, shall we say, was made in regard to an idea; then how to work it out came later. Already we learn of some reservations in this respect. Earlier this year the minister was indefinite about a great many things; now he tells us that it is possible that, in the main, integration or so-called integration, or unification of command, will take place within three years, and that in so far as Canadian forces headquarters is concerned, with the exception of logistics and engineering, by late next fall.

I am not going to say any more about this matter at the present time. We had a complete examination of it earlier this year. Again I am going to make the reservations that I made at that time. I would like to see, in the performance of this reorganization, just what has happened to the civilian counterparts in the minister's office, the alternative that was offered by the opposition with regard to the reorganization in order to eliminate some of the very real difficulties regarding the chain of command as it now exists.
The minister did say something about the replacement of ships for the navy. Well, it is still delightfully vague as to when the decision may be made. The minister will agree, I think, that over the past few months he has been very pleasant and very non-committal when he has been asked by members of the opposition when a certain decision was going to be taken. He has said it would be in a few days, shortly, or in due course; all those nice, imprecise terms. But the minister used to-if I may use a very slang phrase-blow his stack, when he sat in the opposition, if these expressions were used by his predecessors in office. I remember that his indignation used to be something to behold, but he certainly learned the lesson far better than his teachers as to imprecision and this delightful vagueness in so far as telling the house what is being planned is concerned.

I think today the same thing applies with regard to the ships and what he has told us with regard to the decisions taken by him in connection with the Assiniboine and the Nipigon, as well as the Sea King helicopters were also decisions taken much earlier. The conversion of the St. Laurent class of destroyer escorts was an earlier decision. The purchase of the three submarines was also an earlier decision. The only way the minister or this administration can claim that some of these decisions may be theirs is by saying that on assuming office they suspended everything and then decided to reconfirm the decisions.
One thing they have not done, and I think it is very serious. Two years ago the hon. member for Calgary North, when minister of defence, announced a program respecting general purpose frigates. On assuming office the new minister suspended that decision, and then


after several months decided not to go ahead with them. But there has been no announcement whatever as to whether there are to be any ships to replace the general purpose frigates, whether there will be a modification of the proposed general purpose frigates, or what there will be. There is that delightfully vague suggestion concerning ships. Is this suggestion along the line attributed to the associate minister the other day, that there should be ships with great troop carrying capacity; that the transport ability of the navy would be increased? If these remarks were attributed, rightly or wrongly, to the associate minister there may be some validity in the point of view that the navy requires some type of ships which will provide a greater troop carrying capacity in a combined role. I remember the minister's notorious speech in which a bold new military policy was announced. That was the one which sort of spluttered but did not get off the ground. That was a famous occasion which the minister will remember to his dying day.

speechtext: It got off the ground too soon.

speechtext:
It was a damp squib in any event. There was in that statement of policy an item in connection with greater transportability of men and equipment by the navy.
We have not heard too much about the minister's thoughts in this regard. I think that today he could have taken the house into his confidence in connection with what he conceives to be the strategy and tactical use of our Canadian armed forces, particularly the army. In addition, we have not heard about the proposed reorganization of army commands. True enough, the minister said that he is looking at this, but in the interval are our brigades marking time?
I can do nothing but underline the absolute urgency of arriving at a decision regarding replacement ships for the navy. Certainly the defence committee is of the opinion that the decision must be made soon. The committee was made aware, both by the minister's advisers and by the senior officials of those forces with which the navy is co-operating in the north Atlantic, that unless we get some of these replacement ships laid down soon there is going to be a gap by 1970, when the obsolescence of our present ships will place many of them in the category of very limited use.
It must be remembered that the minister's advisers in this regard were primarily the same men who advised the hon. member

for Calgary North and the previous administration on a ship replacement program. They foresaw over two years ago that these ships would have to be replaced, yet two years later we are still in suspense. It is obvious that there is going to be a gap, unless of course their role is going to be changed; but we have heard nothing in that regard. Therefore, assuming their role will remain as it is now, I suggest to the minister that it is high time that the qualitative and quantitative capacity of our navy be decided upon as of now. Not only is it important to our defence capability, but I am sure the minister understands that this question is seriously affecting the morale of the men in the navy, and that there is a limit to their patience in this regard.
The same comments apply to replacement aircraft. There seems to be a sort of self generated hysteria building up in connection with this matter, and I am wondering just how much of this has been sponsored by certain circles in connection with an aircraft to replace the CF-104. One article in this connection which appeared recently was entitled "The Phantom aircraft industry". Then there was a most extraordinary communique put out I know not by whom, but presumably by someone on behalf of the minister, on the eve of the conference of Canadian air industries, in which the air industry was told to mind its P's and Q's. As I say, I do not know who was the spokesman but certainly it appeared to be someone in authority.
The following week, namely the week of October 7, the chief of the Canadian defence staff reportedly said in Quebec city that the air defence order is still being worked out. As far as the defence committee is concerned, if the minister feels that some of his opinions should not be made public and wants to come before that committee in camera, I think the defence committee is quite a responsible body which has in the past been able to sit in camera and treat the information placed before it as confidential and for its benefit only.
According to some stories which have appeared in the press there is a tug of war going on in the defence department. There are protagonists of a very fancy and sophisticated aircraft, the McDonnell Phantom fighter, known as a $2.5 million, eight ton bomb carrier. At least that is how it is headed up.
I have also received reports concerning a number of other aircraft, or what one might term potential candidates. No doubt history
Supply-National Defence is repeating itself and there is no dearth of potential candidates. I have referred to the Phantom II. I understand one other candidate is the Northrop Freedom Fighter, which is reportedly less expensive, being in the neighbourhood of $600,000 per copy. There is also the Grumman Intruder, referred to in one press report as an extraordinary ground support aircraft at an extraordinary cost, $4 million per copy. Even that cost is nothing compared to what the Arrow was going to cost. There is also the Douglas Sky Hawk, the Thunderchief and the Lougheed CL-90, which is presumably akin to the CF-104 or the model on which that aircraft was based.
Mr. Chairman, there are two aspects to the philosophy of such a choice. We must consider the glamourous side, shall we say, of the former air force. We cannot call it the air force any more because it has been taken into this integrated force, or so some people believe. In this regard one must consider the Phantom II whish is reportely to be a very slick, complex aircraft. As I indicated some days ago, some individuals have suggested that an informal agreement has been reached and all that is required now is an agreement among Britain, the United States and Canada for the manufacture of airframes in Canada, some 250 I believe. The aircraft would have a British engine, which could be substituted for an engine of United States manufacture. This is all speculation, and, undoubtedly, there is uncertainty in this regard. However, the source of this report is usually reasonable and authoritative. Where there is smoke there is usually a certain amount of fire.
Mr. Chairman, it may well be that this proposition is being examined carefully. The Phantom II is reputed to be a very fast aircraft with a speed of something like 1,600 miles per hour, with a 900 mile range and an eight ton bomb carrying capacity. I think one must also consider the Northrop Freedom Fighter, which is described as a $700,000 grass field jet. It is a much more versatile aircraft for the tactical role. I understand the Phantom II requires a runway of some 5,000 feet. In any event, there are two conflicting philosophies in this regard. One is that we need a more or less workaday jeep type aircraft, and the other is that we must have an aircraft which is in the Cadillac class.
Mr. Chairman, I point out these facts because there seems to be some indication that the minister and his advisers are considering the continuation of a tactical role
9846	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence lor at least a good segment of our air force. We should like to know the official philosophy in regard to the utilization of our air component with our ground forces. Is the use of our air component concentrated on transportability? There are varying views in this regard. We could use our air component in such a way as to make sure our ground troops are transported to certain areas, making them highly mobile. In that event their equipment and logistics supplies would be readily transportable. This use of our forces would fit into the Canadian peace keeping role to be utilized at any place in the world where it was required. In contrast to that role is the use of a substantial part of our air component as an air arm combined with ground forces.
There are two very different principles involved and, of course, very different consequences. A tactical air arm would require tactical aircraft with necessarily shorter ranges. If we are going to use that type of aircraft in conjunction with our forces stationed some distance from Canada one must be concerned about getting the short range aircraft to a place within the limit of their range from our forces.
As I have said, I do not intend to go into detail in relation to the consequences of this philosophy, as time does not permit, but I point out these facts as fundamental differ-rences in respect of the potential role of the air component of Canada's defence forces. Certainly a judgment decision will have to be reached, and we should like to know the thoughts of the minister in this regard. A decision in respect of replacement aircraft in this particular range is forecast in the minister's remarks. He says he hopes to be able to arrive at a decision concerning tactical aircraft, perhaps not within a few weeks but in the near future. The two week period had reference to the shipbuilding program. In any event "the near future" is a relative term. The officials involved certainly are considering the situation.
Other remarks have been attributed to the minister to the effect that he will reply to the aircraft industry but that his decision may well be a year away, and that the industry should not push or rush him. We should have some clarification in this regard. I am pleased to note that steps are being taken toward the use of the C-130. I always felt that we were a little hesitant in buying only four of these aircraft, but there were several factors involved. Perhaps for another reason


the limited purchase of this aircraft proved useful in that it has been shown that these aircraft can really deliver the goods without the necessity of obtaining an expensive air fleet. The hesitancy in this regard has resulted in the continued use of C-119's to the point where one wondered how they could still fly.
I should like to hear from the minister about the modified version of the Caribou, now called the Buffalo. What does the Canadian Department of National Defence envisage in respect of this development? Is this to be a Canadian development encouraged chiefly by the United States? I think we must realize that in so far as the Buffalo is concerned, it was not developed as a result of Canadian encouragement. It was ultimately brought into production in its refined state- or an improvement upon the Caribou

as a result of encouragement from a source other than Canadian. I was sorry that we were unable to see our way clear to follow the original concept of the Caribou and the Bobcat in a more closely related role. In any event, I am sure that we have been taught a lesson by our mistakes and I trust we will not repeat them.
The minister should make reference in his reply to a replacement for the Penhold air base. After all, Penhold was supposed to be the chief centre for advanced jet training. This plan was knocked on the head rather unceremoniously and I think improperly. True enough, the minister felt bound by certain decisions reached within the Department of Transport, but these decisions have sufficient against them to render them somewhat suspect. In any event, there it is; the minister has announced that the Penhold air base is to be closed. What is to be its replacement, we have not heard. I think there should be some indication of what the plan is in so far as training command is concerned. Is this going to await some uncertain date in the future when everything is going to be reorganized?
Now, I did hear in passing that the minister's introductory statement made no reference to the militia. I too regret that he failed to mention this. True enough he made his statement to the defence committee, but I think the militia merited as much mention publicly as did the Cyprus force. I agree with the minister that our force on Cyprus has performed very well under very trying and frustrating circumstances. I think we must give them full marks in that regard. Mind you, I cannot approve of the circumstances under which they had to perform their duties.

I think, too, the minister will agree that the organization of our peace keeping force in these international groups leaves something to be desired. I am hoping that the conference this week will be able to iron out a lot of these difficulties. These people who have been to Cyprus, and who have come back, will readily testify that such peace keeping forces have far too many chiefs and not enough men. At every level we seem to require equivalent officers from each participating nation. I believe experience will lead us to the point where these peace keeping forces can be organized on the basis of efficiency and not prestige.
With regard to the militia, I should like to read into the record paragraphs 70 and 72 of the defence committee report:
There was considerable discussion in the committee concerning the numbers required to fulfil these roles.
The reference there is to the roles the government indicated for the militia.
The government has indicated a requirement of
30.000	effective militiamen as follows:
(a)	reinforcement of field forces, 7,000-8,000 officers and men; special units for NATO commitments, 1,000 officers and men;
(b)	training forces to support the field force,
18.000	officers and men;
(c)	internal security, 2,500 officers and men;
(d)	national survival installations, 1,500 officers and men, for a total of approximately 30,000 officers and men.
Then the committee's remarks follow:
Your committee cannot confirm or refute this estimate except to note that the potential requirement for internal security appears to be seriously underestimated. Your committee also recognizes the fact that those requirements will change in the future, and that regular periodic reviews should be made.
Then I quote paragraph 72:
The government has announced that the present strength of the militia is to be cut, for budgetary reasons, from approximately 45,000 all ranks to approximately 30,000. To achieve the requirement of 30,000 referred to in paragraph 70, this would mean an approximately 100 per cent efficiency rate. Your committee considers this to be unrealistic- I
I can assure the minister, without disclosing what went on in the committee, that this was an almost unanimous view.
-and would agree with the contention of the conference of defence associations, that in order to achieve the 30,000 effectives, the militia enrolment, even taking into account an increased efficiency, would have to be considerably higher. It must therefore be recognized that, after the militia is cut to 30,000 all ranks, it will be unable to fulfil its proposed roles.

I wish to thank hon. members for their courtesy in allowing me to have a few more minutes to complete my remarks. We did have a bit of a comic opera performance with regard to this matter this summer. It was announced that the 30,000 figure was going to be the end result. The minister's associate indicated that he would have to agree with the contention in the committee and the conference of defence associations that undoubtedly enrolment would have to be somewhat higher. He was not precise because one could not precisely indicate what that higher figure might be, but certainly it would be higher than 30,000. However, on a subsequent appearance the associate minister indicated that there was a hard line adopted, and 30,000 was going to be it.
Then we had the minister come before us the other day and say that the 30,000 figure still held but there would be an establishment of some 41,000. In response to questioning in the committee the minister agreed that in the implementation of this proposal it would be possible to get up to a figure of 41,000 if everybody enlisted up to the top and if they could get the money, which is another consideration, but he thought 30,000 would be the practical figure.
I believe he will agree with me that if he wants to get 30,000 men out of the militia, as set out in paragraph 70 of the defence committee report-those figures were taken straight from the ministerial statement in this regard, so there is no hocus-pocus or glossing over of the figures by the committee-he will not get 30,000 out of a 30,000 enrolment. Something has got to give. Perhaps the minister might be a little more frank with the committee and tell us just how many men he thinks he is going to get out of a militia force of 30,000.
I am going to leave to some of my colleagues the discussion of what may be the effects of the militia reorganization. However, there is one last point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman, at this stage of my remarks.

Supply-National Defence I do not claim originality for this idea, but I think it should be put to the minister, perhaps not so much to the minister as to some of his colleagues. As was indicated the other day, as a result of this reorganization of the militia, the reserves and the regular force, certain national defence properties are going to be surplus. What properties will become surplus is not yet determined. We know what happens when these properties are declared surplus; they are turned over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for sale. The proceeds of the sale are then credited to the consolidated revenue fund.
I know that in my own city of Edmonton there may be several hundred thousand dollars worth of property that will go on the market, and it should. There are a number of lots there that are producing nothing but the best weed crop possible. They are surrounded by a fence and posted with signs saying "No Admittance, Department of National Defence". Neither is there admittance for a weed cutter. I am sure the situation is paralleled in a number of other cities, and that there is property worth hundreds of thousands of dollars which could be disposed of by the department.
Admittedly the minister is short of funds for the purchase of new equipment. If, by reason of the Financial Administration Act, it is impossible to take the funds realized from the sale of these properties and return them to the department for the purchase of new equipment, then I suggest an agreement should be reached with the minister's colleagues that he be provided with an extra credit in lieu of the amount realized. This makes sense, because in effect he would be disposing of properties that were purchased by his department.
This idea is not original but it is a commendable one, and I think the minister's colleagues should see the wisdom in it. I am sure the minister himself advocates this, and it can be pointed out that it is a one shot proposition because he will not be able to continue to find properties that can be sold.
I may have some other remarks to make depending on the minister's answers to questions raised, but for the moment that is all I have to say.

speechtext:
You will find it there, but today the minister made no statement on the policy position of the government with respect to nuclear weapons and nuclear warheads. I believe we should have had some indication from him as to the policy of the government with regard to the role of Canada's armed forces in the use of nuclear weapons.
A second matter which the minister omitted to mention

and I hope he will not shake his head at this too-was that the government undertook to renegotiate the position of Canada within NATO. That was not only a campaign promise but is also to be found in Hansard, and the minister made no mention of it today. I know he made certain statements about NATO, but he did not go into the fundamental principle and philosophy of Canada's role within the NATO structure.
Up until now I have always supported Canada's contribution to NATO, but surely the time has arrived when the minister should tell us in detail what he has in mind for the future. If memory serves me correctly 1969 is the year for the re-establishment of NATO as a collective military alliance, and tied in with this question of NATO itself is the other question of how long Canada is to continue

maintaining thousands of its troops, at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars, in the European theatre. V-E day was the day the surrender was signed in Berlin. That was may 8, 1945. We are now in November of 1964. Have our operations in Europe in the interval been considered as peace keeping? Was there any thought in the mind of the government when the surrender was signed in 1945 that in 1964 a small country of 19 million people would still be supporting occupation forces in Europe at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars?
I think this is a reasonable and logical question to ask, and one with regard to which we should have some information. We are entitled to have the views of the Minister of National Defence on this matter. I should be grateful, too, if the minister would indicate how he intends to implement the policy set out on page 15 of the white paper, the policy on peace keeping, in the light of what is contained on page 24 where priorities are outlined.
The white paper was interesting enough, but basically it deals in generalities. Even where it is detailed, how are the aims set out in the white paper to be accomplished having regard to the availability of Canadian forces and funds? Beyond this, bearing in mind the money available, what kind of efficiency are we to expect in our armed services? We are at peace, thank heavens, but it is amazing how much money Canada can spend through the Department of National Defence while the country is at peace. If my recollection is accurate, between 1949 and the end of 1963 the Department of National Defence spent $22J billion on our armed services. And what is their efficiency? Now is the time to bring this question out into the open.
I had the honour of being leader of the opposition in British Columbia while Canada was at war. As leader of the opposition I had the privilege, along with the premier of British Columbia and the G.O.C. western command, of knowing what was going on. But because of public relations psychology I could never make known what I knew then, namely, some passenger ships with naval personnel on board carried guns made of wood. This was when Japan was in the war. I knew this, but I could not say so because we were at war and it would not have been advisable. But we are at peace now, and we should be able to discuss the efficiency 20220-623J
Supply-National Defence of our forces. I heard nothing from the minister about this aspect of our defence situation.
I had hoped to hear about that naval exercise off Bermuda when three Canadian destroyers took part in combined operations with the United States navy Atlantic command. Members of the special committee on defence set up by this House of Commons were aboard the three Canadian destroyers taking part in this actual, factual exercise. There were three destroyers in line. I happened to be one of those on the first destroyer in line. What armament did those destroyers carry? They had a mortar for use against submarines, and they had only one piece of armament equipment for everything else, a 3 inch-70 guns for use against attacking forces or attacking planes. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that this was a prearranged exercise; it had been on the books for a long time. The department knew members of the defence committee would be present, so I imagine everything was ice cream and perfect.
What happened? In the beautiful, calm waters off Bermuda, when the drone plane flew over, the only armament available for use against an attacking force would function to the extent of only about 50 per cent. One of the guns aboard the destroyer I was on would not fire. We had that experience. The gun on the second destroyer would not fire at all on two runs. Aboard the third they were luckier. Remember, this was shooting at a drone plane; and the only armament carried would not function to more than 50 per cent of capacity. Would the minister say these ships are ready for war if it ever occurs? We were told these guns were the most intricate and complicated in the world, but they are the only guns provided, and this is the situation.
Surely we have a responsibility as well as a right to ask the minister now what is being done in this regard. Is the armament being changed? I understand there is an arrangement with Britain for skilled men to come over here to assist us with our submarine program. Does the minister not think there should be a similar arrangement for technical assistance in connection with these guns? Or should there be a change of armament? Remember this is the only armament those destroyers possess apart from the mortars which are only for use against submarines. Now we are at peace I think we should be absolutely honest, and that we are entitled to expect honesty from the minister.
May I call it one o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee recessed at one o'clock I was speaking about the fantastic expenditures of the Department of National Defence amounting, as I pointed out, to $22J billion since 1949, and my own experience as a member of the defence committee in finding out the inefficiency of some armaments, despite these expenditures. If time permitted I would have liked to have the opportunity of enlarging on that phase of my remarks, because I think to a considerable degree it applies to the armaments, and in particular the mobility of our forces at home and abroad. However, in view of the fact that you were kind enough, Mr, Chairman, when I spoke to you a moment ago, to let me know that I now have 13J minutes left, I would like to proceed from that phase of my remarks on item 1 of the estimates of the Department of National Defence to another matter which I mentioned at the opening of my remarks relative to our position regarding NATO, and in particular to what I maintain was the lack of responsibility by the Minister of National Defence in not outlining to this house what we should have had, and had the right to expect, namely an explanation of his policy statement which is to be found on page 15 of the white paper on defence, correlated with the priorities as outlined on page 24 of the white paper.
During my very brief remarks before the luncheon adjournment with regard to NATO I rather gathered from the expression on the face of the Minister of National Defence that he thought I might have been a little out of line. May I draw to the attention of this committee a press release covering the text of a speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Atlantic treaty association at Ottawa on September 15, 1964. On page 4 of the press release we find the Secretary of State for External Affairs saying this:
As far as the alliance itself is concerned, there is still a long way to go toward completion of the review of NATO defence policy which ministers required at the Ottawa meeting in May, 1963. While I would not wish to overstress the problems of the alliance in that regard, I cannot escape the feeling that the long term effects of not achieving some agreement in the fields of strategy, military integration, nuclear control, command structure and cost sharing are bound to detract from our effectiveness as an alliance in using the forces we have at our disposal. I believe that the time has come to face these problems and honestly to deal with them with the requisite boldness and imagination. In particular I believe

that they point to the need for some re-thinking first with regard to a greater sharing in the military direction of the alliance, and second, in regard to the relationship between the civilian and military arms of the alliance.
Mr. Chairman, you will remember that when I spoke before the luncheon adjournment I expressed my regret that the Minister of National Defence had not given us any basic point of view or policy outline with regard to what I said then was a re-thinking of our position in NATO and its operations. That is why this afternoon, because I believed my memory was correct, I looked into my files; I was almost certain that a similar expression had been used by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his speech on September 15. Members of this House of Commons are not children; they have responsibilities-big ones-and one concerns the relationship of our country to others, and the defence of our country. But for some reason or other there was an evasion of rationalization and no attempt whatsoever by the Minister of National Defence, in his introduction with regard to item No. 1 of these estimates, to take this house or the people into his confidence, into the government's confidence, on the major issues that face our country and others. Nor was there an attempt to give us an explanation as to how in his view, believing as he must in the general principles of peace keeping as outlined on page 15 of the white paper, we could follow the priorities set out on page 24 without a massive increase in defence expenditure or a cut down in other fields.
In the few remaining moments I want to speak on the cutting down in other fields. As I said this morning the surrender treaty was signed in Europe in 1945. Today we are still spending hundreds of millions of dollars, and have thousands of troops. For how long is this going to go on? Is it peace keeping? I would also like to be able to quote all of the observations on page 15, but may I just very briefly draw attention to this paragraph, which I presume reflects the views of the Minister of National Defence:
Canada's own experience in this field points to the need for a high degree of versatility in preparing for possible United Nations service. In the past, requests from the secretary general for assistance have been for specialists of various kinds, mainly from the Canadian army and the R.C.A.F.-
The success of United Nations peace keeping operations may depend on the speed with which they can be established on the ground. Once there, they may be required to exercise authority with limited personnel in broad areas. Thus, there is

a need for mobility as regards deployment, method of operation and logistic support. In most situations which can be foreseen, there is likely to be a need for highly mobile forces for ground observation, air surveillance, rapid transportation and reliable communications. These are among the United Nations requirements which Canadian forces have helped to meet in the past.
As I read the white paper, emphasis is to be placed on peace keeping and greater aid through the medium of the United Nations. That is why there is the requirement in the priorities listed on page 24 that:
On the basis of this assessment, major expenditures in the next few years will be designed to: (a) re-equip the army as a mobile force; (b) provide an adequate air and sea lift for its immediate deployment in an emergency; (e) acquire tactical aircraft; (d) maintain a relatively constant improvement of maritime antisubmarine capability.
I believe with regard to (d) that the minister is doing an excellent job. With regard to (a), (b) and (c) heavy financial requirements will be necessary to meet these objectives.
I honour the Minister of National Defence for the approach he has made toward integrating the forces. That is an experiment which is being watched around the world. I think he is to be commended for the courage he has shown in some of the new approaches which are being made. At the same time, sir, I think that he did a disservice to the members of this house by not stating whether or not these savings which he hopes to accomplish can or will meet what he states in the white paper to be his objectives. In not giving us that information he failed to give the complete picture regarding our continued operation on the present basis within the commitments of NATO and particularly in connection with NORAD.
I was most interested in what he had to say about the two Bomarc installations in Canada, one in Ontario and one in Quebec. I noted his remarks to the effect that the interceptors at Comox are going to have nuclear warheads. I say it is time we had some honesty both from the minister and from this government. Up till now we have had only what I maintain is dishonesty in certain matters of policy. Is the minister actually telling this committee that in the event of an attack on the North American continent the enemy would give warning of the approach of manned bombers so as to give the United States time to get its I.C.B.M.'s on their way? And on the other side of the picture-I know this will not happen but I put it hypothetically-if the United States ever attacked the U.S.S.R., do you think that
Supply-National Defence it would send its manned bombers and give the Russians time to get their I.C.B.M.'s on their way to North America? Of course not.
That being the case-and surely that is logical and reasonable-what is the basis for Canada spending money as it is today on Bomarc bases and nuclear warheads for interceptors? What is the basis for the millions which Canada is spending now on NORAD, with this change in technological warfare and the staff which is available? In the past it has been necessary for one purpose-to see that the strategic air command of the United States was kept up in the air. But surely that is not the position today in the event of war. Fifty per cent of the strength of the strategic air command of the United States is up in the air all the time as it is; but it can only meet manned bombers. Surely it is time we had an explanation from the minister of the necessity for spending millions of dollars and utilizing Canadian personnel on Bomarc stations, nuclear warheads, interceptors and NORAD, all of which would be of use only in the event of attack by manned bombers. I might add, although this has no connection with NORAD, that this month saw the completion of four stations outside of Canada to detect the launching of an I.C.B.M. anywhere in the world.
I am down to my last 30 seconds, Mr. Chairman, and I do not want to take additional time. Perhaps I will have an opportunity later to speak again, but may I conclude my remarks by saying what I said at the outset. There was no reference to matters of policy or matters of viewpoint and no indication of the government's understanding of the objectives given in the statement made by the Minister of National Defence. Such being the case the minister has shown disrespect for and disregard of the members of this committee and the responsibilities each and every one of us has as a member of this House of Commons. Before we are through with these estimates I hope we will have a clear exposition by the minister, and that he will take all of us into his and the government's confidence.
