speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to draw to the attention of the house a situation which I deplore at the present time. Today, the house is taking up the estimates of the Department of National Defence, which represent 25 per cent of Canada's national budget; and even though the matter is a rather touchy one, and
98S2

Supply-National Defence one that is discussed at length during electoral campaigns here and there across the country, very few members of the house are interested in discussing it when it comes up for debate in the house.
I think that the absence of the members of the defence committee from the house is particularly unfortunate. The 24 members who have been chosen by the House of Commons and by the various parties to scrutinize the national defence problem in this country as well as the financial impact of national defence are surely of all the members of this parliament the ones who should deem it their duty to be here today.
This being said, must we come to the conclusion that the defence committee have Ho more work to do once they have completed their study outside the house, and that their members ought not take part in the discussions that can go on in this house? I hope not.
This committee did a good job by allowing several members to examine thoroughly the very complex problem of defence. And the house could thus avoid momentarily the discussions on national defence which we have known in the past.
During the first session I sat in this house, in 1962, I remember that almost every day questions were being placed on the order paper concerning national defence. I remember that long discussions and debates occurred on this question. At least, since the committee on national defence was formed to examine this matter, those discussions calmed down in the house. Sometimes several weeks go by without the Minister of National Defence having to answer any questions from members of the opposition.
We have at least attained that objective. But, in my opinion, when the estimates of the Department of National Defence are examined in the house, it is the duty of every member, Conservative and others, to attend the debate, because this matter affects a very important area, not only at the economic but also at the social level; many Canadians are thereby affected directly: those in the armed forces, and indirectly, their dependents. And I could also add all the taxpayers who foot the bill at the end of the year.
In his statement the minister outlined the general policy which the cabinet intends to apply concerning defence. Of course, he did not have much information for us, members of the committee, except that there are still many questions unanswered, including the

one raised a while ago by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch).
I think that the Minister of National Defence did not give us exactly what we had a right to expect.
When he talks about maintaining NORAD agreements for the defence of the North American continent, with the United States, does he mean to maintain them exactly on the basis which has prevailed since 1957? Will he renegotiate the agreements when they come to an end?
I think that we are all in agreement in this house-and all Canadians will support the suggestion-that we must maintain our contribution to the defence of the North American continent. But I think it is proper for Canadians to wonder on what basis it will be.
We are all aware, because it was repeated many times, that our present system of defence is simply out of date and obsolete. Therefore, when we talk about the defence of the North American continent what are we talking about exactly? Before setting up defence policies it would be a good thing to know exactly what threat we have to face. Are we facing an invasion by some foreign force on the continent? Are we facing an air force attack? Or is there a danger for Canada to be destroyed by remote controlled nuclear head missiles?
I believe that it is easy to determine what type of war or attack could take place against Canada.
It is quite unlikely that we would be faced with an invasion of land forces, since, for more than 300 years now, no sizeable enemy has ever set foot on our Canadian soil, with the exception of small raids by the American people at the beginning of the last century.
It is unrealistic, in my opinion, to maintain some of our present defence items when we all agree that they would be inefficient against the only threat really conceivable.
We have Bomarc bases. Now, we all know that these bases do not represent actually any kind of protection. Yet, we continue to maintain them, perhaps, to please our allies across the border. We maintain squadrons of Voodoos equipped with nuclear missiles.
Have we fully realized the extent of the threat that is hanging over us? There again I very much doubt it, because in the light of all the information we have been able to get in the committee on defence, it is more obvious every day that an attack would not

be launched against our continent by long-range bombers.
Therefore, once again we are clearly behind the times.
I know that the minister has discarded two squadrons and reduced that force of Voodoo aircraft to three squadrons only. Of course, that was a step in the right direction, but that does not solve the problem at all, because I think the whole problem is based on the following question: What will the next war be like and what will be its pattern?
In co-operation with the Americans, we have developed a radar system which had to be discarded as soon as, if not before, it was completed, because several radar stations, all across the country, were closed during the last year. I am a little amazed to notice that we closed radar stations and that actually, we are building some others. It is quite difficult to reconcile those rather extreme positions.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) was obviously referring to the promises made by the Liberal party during the last election campaign when he mentioned that, after coming to power, this government was supposed to renegotiate the agreements signed with the U.S.A. by its predecessor with respect to North American defence and also Canada's role within NATO.
What has the government done in the two years it has been in power? Has it renegotiated anything? Of course, it will argue that the agreements in question have not yet expired but, in my opinion, one does not have to wait until agreements have expired to renegotiate them. The government must decide what policy it will follow when those agreements come to an end.
While I am on the subject of NATO and of Canada's role within the alliance, I might say that I had the privilege of visiting our bases in Europe. Like the other members of the defence committee, I was in a position to realize the importance of Canada's presence on the old continent, but I must say that that importance is more psychological than military because, 20 years after the war, our presence there is more or less necessary, in my opinion. I am not advocating Canada's full withdrawal from NATO, but I feel that we should be active in all organizations. What should be our role? It should be adapted to our capabilities and to actual needs. In the last year we have undertaken, as Canadians, to build up a much more mobile military force which could be put at the disposal of the United Nations. I think this is a good
Supply-National Defence thing, even if it may present certain negative aspects.
I believe that our sense of responsibility compels us to take that course but, personally, if I consider the part we are called to play in NATO and our intention to increase our contribution to the United Nations, I feel it would be logical to conclude that we should reduce our NATO expenses in proportion to the intended increase in United Nations contribution, since these two organizations complete one another, to a certain extent. In my opinion, it is rather difficult to justify a double expense for the same purpose.
Considering that European nations such as France, Germany, Belgium, Holland, England and Italy regained an economic stability and a power which cannot be doubted and which are clearly superior to ours, I think it is logical for Canada to reduce its contribution to NATO and, like the great majority of Canadians, I would be pleased to see a reduction in our armed forces within NATO.
Considering our commitments, I think Canada should get ready, when these commitments are fulfilled to withdraw the major part of its military forces in Europe, leaving a nucleus of officers charged with co-ordinating the work of the soldiers in Europe and with keeping the military forces in Canada and Canadian authorities aware of any development which might occur on the European continent.
The minister spoke about the CF-104 supersonic aircraft stationed in Europe. We have all had to decide, for some time, not to renew these aircraft. If we consider the role assigned to such aircraft, I believe that the decision not to replace them is logical, and that it is also logical to conclude that our participation in the air forces of NATO should be abandoned upon the expiry of our commitments. France, Britain, Germany and Italy are sufficiently strong now to replace the few squadrons we still have left on that continent.
I believe that there is a point here that we must consider, a rather important point which is raised by our presence in Europe. It is the human aspect of the matter. It is the sacrifice required from those thousands of Canadians in Europe who have to live away from their family, their parents, their environment, their country. Several have their family with them but this is not the case for the majority. I feel there is a human problem there. In my opinion, it is illogical, in the circumstances, to maintain in Europe

Supply-National Defence a force which, for all practical purposes, cannot be justified.
There is also another aspect to consider: the expenditures which contribute to increase to a certain point our trade monetary deficit with the other countries. Canada's balance of trade is unfavourable, and it is obvious that all expenses made in other countries by Canadians increase this deficit. Even though we ship the majority of equipment and provisions for our troops in Europe, it remains that these people spend a lot of money in those countries and that the Canadian treasury must pay to keep them there.
We are all in favour of a greater role for Canada in peace keeping operations. I think the action taken by our country during the Cyprus crisis proves our willingness to solve that problem even in other parts of the world.
I believe the experience of Canada in Cyprus will serve in other circumstances. Personally, I think Canada has reason to be proud of its contribution in that part of the world.
I should like to say a few words about our navy. It seems to me that, for the past few years, our navy has been somewhat neglected, with the result that, today, we are faced with a rather sad situation, and by that I mean that we now have a navy whose definitely obsolete equipment is not suited to the tasks we intend to assign to it. There is no doubt that before purchasing equipment for our navy, we should determine what part we mean it to play.
At present, following all those discussions, the committee is aware that the military role of the Canadian navy is extremely limited. Our coast line is quite extensive and we Canadians cannot expect our present navy to be able to guard and keep watch efficiently over all our shores.
It would therefore be impractical to consider such a possibility. We must also ask ourselves if, should a conflict occur, it would be fought at sea. We have all recognized that, in case of war, the battle is not very likely to take place at sea. A little of it at first, perhaps, but for such a short while that our ships would hardly have time to weigh anchor. This raises the question of whether a navy is justified for the defence of our country.
The defence committee decided that the only role our navy could play would be to destroy submarines. It is quite clear that our navy could play an important part in the

detection of submarines, but I feel there is all the difference in the world between detecting a submarine and preventing it from attacking.
In fact, if we compare the features of a submarine with those of a surface ship, namely speed, depth and period of immersion, mobility, armaments, I am of the opinion that the submarine has more advantages than the surface ship.
Moreover, I think that if we had to face a war in which atomic submarines would play a part, our surface ships would be definitely in an inferior situation and we would suffer heavy losses, notwithstanding the few gains we might achieve.
Does that mean that we must give up any role in that field? Of course, I do not believe so, but we must try to limit ourselves to probabilities and possibilities, and in my opinion, the submarine detection system seems better when it is operated by airplanes and their radar systems.
If we take into consideration the fact that a destroyer may cost $10, $15 and even $20 million, according to its shape and class, and that an Argus or Neptune airplane may cost half a million, a million or $2 million; in short, if we consider the work that one may do as compared with the other, I feel that we may easily conclude that for the amounts of money available in this field, it is definitely better to increase the number of aircraft for air patrol, rather than increase the number of destroyers. It would be easier for the enemy to destroy a surface destroyer than a flying aircraft.
On the other hand, if we consider the possibility of patrolling a wide area, again the aircraft has definite advantages over the destroyer.
It has been argued that an aircraft has limited means to destroy the enemy. I think that it is true, but under the circumstances, it must also be admitted that the destroyer has also very limited means to destroy a submarine.
There is also another aspect which must be considered. When an atomic submarine is given the order to take part in a conflict, it is most probable that its only warning will be a guided missile with nuclear warhead. I feel that it is illogical to think that we can prevent a submarine from firing its missiles; even if we know its location, those destructive missiles will be ready to be fired when orders are given and even if it is destroyed afterwards, I do not think that this will make much difference in the results.

There is also something else to be considered. The purpose of a submarine is to destroy populated and industrial centres of our continent. It would surely not attack a ship because such prey is not worthwhile. If it attacks anything, it will surely be highly populated cities, administrative and industrial centres of the continent. What will be the use then of destroyers, even on the surface, if we no longer have administrative centres in Canada, if the population is partly destroyed?
At that time, our ships will have to remain at sea, unable to return to their home ports, since they will have been destroyed.
It is therefore illogical to recommend increased expenses in the naval service. However, I must recognize that the personnel of our armed forces is very well disciplined and trained, and that we can be proud of them. But I wonder whether to experience such pride, we should spend $1 billion, $1J billion or $lf billion a year, to maintain those fine sporting clubs and to allow those young men to indulge their taste for adventure at sea? Should we spend yearly $200 or $300 million to provide them with toys with which they may play?
I believe this is a question we should ask ourselves. If the navy plays a necessary role, if there is need for it, in brief, if the threat to our security is real, then, there can be no question of money. Should our country be threatened, the point is not to ask ourselves what we can do, but what we must do. But at this time, we are unable to establish exactly the magnitude of this threat, and even less how we can face it.
Mr. Chairman, the expenditures of the Department of National Defence at present account for about one quarter of the national budget. I believe drastic cuts will have to be made, for its present spending is in no way commensurate with the aims sought.
Other questions obviously have to be considered in connection with the curtailment of the national defence budget, and I know that the minister himself has been severely criticized for some cuts in some particular fields.
The military establishment has been brought down to 10,000, and the minister was criticized for this action. He closed down radar stations, military bases all over the country, and for that too he was sharply criticized. Economic consequences on our economy of military expenditures will have, of course, to be considered.
Committee members have received reports about studies they had requested, precisely with regard to the economic implications of
Supply-National Defence military expenditures on the country and also to the economic consequences in case of world disarmament.
We know that throughout the world countries are now studying the possible economic implications of an international agreement on total disarmament. I feel that this is a matter the study of which will be most interesting, and, so far as I am concerned, I feel sure that the members of the committee will devote much of their time to its study; for it is a problem that must be faced, considering the criticism which resulted from the cuts in military personnel and expenditures in certain sections of the country.
We all hope that military expenditures will be reduced, provided it does not affect us personally. However, I feel we should be more realistic and recognize that, if certain cuts can be made in military expenditures, we must also find ways of spending money in other fields which will be more productive and will contribute to increase the value of our country as a whole.
It is, of course, very easy to criticize, but it is much more difficult to achieve something. I know that the Minister of National Defence is conscious not only of the problem as such, but of its magnitude; as far as I am concerned, and like all the other members indeed, I shall support any suggestion tending to the reduction of military expenditures, in accordance with our abilities, while maintaining the part we should logically play in the free world's defence.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak today on behalf of the Rallie-ment Creditiste on the estimates of the Department of National Defence, but I have changed my mind. I wish to deal with an aspect of the matter different from what we have heard so far this afternoon. I hope you will permit me at this time, Mr. Chairman, to pay homage to those of our fellow men who fought for this country, especially those who were called by the Department of National Defence when things were dark both in Canada and across the world. I am referring to our veterans, those who made the supreme sacrifice of their lives, in the service of this country. I notice the minister is wearing a poppy today. I am sure he calls to mind various poems and writings which arose out of those days of turmoil. Indeed one of these poems comes to my mind now-the one of John McCrae which contains these familiar words:

Supply-National Defence
In Flanders fields the poppies blow
Between the crosses row on row.
I realize this has only an indirect connection with the estimates which are before us. But were it not for the Department of National Defence I imagine there would not be a Department of Veterans Affairs. This is the aspect to which I wish to devote some time this afternoon.
We have been talking about 25 pages of expenditure. We have been talking about figures, acceptances, transformation, integration, and so on. But we have not heard very much about the moral aspect of this whole question, something which cannot be evaluated in the book of expenditures, something which cannot be divided into subsections. It is a quality one is born with; it is the understanding and the comprehension we should have among ourselves and which nations should have among themselves. We shall be celebrating Remembrance day very soon, a time that affords a good opportunity to remember what has gone by. However, I do not think we should remember our veterans only on one special occasion. I am asking the minister as well as all those in his department and all those in this Canadian parliament that we should bear them in mind throughout the year.
The decisions which the minister has to take are, I am sure, not taken lightly. But we often forget the human side of the whole picture. We may discuss the steps which should be taken to promote the greater efficiency of our armed forces, but let us not forget one thing-if there is a war, if there is turmoil, somebody is responsible for it. It was not in the divine plan that nations should be forever quarrelling with each other; that is not in accordance with the natural law. Wars and conflicts are caused by some organization somewhere which does not agree with the principles being followed by another organization. If today there is a state of crisis between Turkey and Greece, this situation came about as a result of their legislation, as a result of their ways of living, which in turn resulted in strain, misunderstanding and, finally, bloodshed. This is not something new, but perhaps if we appreciate it more fully we may take a different attitude toward the whole of our military set-up. We buy, we plan, we produce and we build to defend ourselves against an enemy; to defend ourselves against an attack from a nation which may not agree with our views. Or else we try to help out our neighbours, as we are doing in Cyprus.

But when will we arm ourselves to fight at home? There is a fight to be fought here, too; a fight which is not carried on with cannon or atomic bombs. In this country as well as abroad I think the best war which can be fought is the war against misery, against incomprehension, against the lack of understanding which exists among nations. It is the fight against misery and poverty in our own country. If we were to abolish many of these sore spots we might save ourselves a great many of the 25 pages we are now considering in the estimates book. The evils I have just mentioned are, basically, the reasons why nations rise up against each other. Something is missing at home.
It would be the same in Canada if the situation which prevails here now were aggravated. I am talking about hunger, about misery, about social insecurity. These were the conditions which prevailed in Germany before the last world war; these were the conditions which prevailed in Cuba. And until we arm ourselves to fight this general enemy we shall have this issue to face; we shall always need arms to defend ourselves, not only against other nations but even against our own people. Legislation flows from this building and we are responsible for it. We in this parliament as well as those in other parliaments across the world are the guiding lights of the nations. Decisions are taken in parliament by human beings, by responsible men. I believe we have too often forgotten those enemies which are not fought with guns or with ammunition. This is the direction in which we need to concentrate our efforts, here at home, and right now. I think possibly that the government understands this, but it is not making a strong enough effort.
The minister had a great deal of information to give the house today. He gave us many details, but they were all related to the same picture, a material picture. I know that the generals, the wing commanders and so on have their needs. They will speak to the minister about them. But they are willing accomplices; they have a job to do and they will ask for the equipment to do that job. I ask this question, though: To what extent is their job necessary? A picture has to be complete, but if it does not fit on the wall it is out of place, no matter what kind of picture it is. It is the whole room one has to look at, not just the picture. Right now I am thinking of the affairs of this nation as a whole. I am wondering whether the minister of defence would cut down his budget-

I do not know about $1, but at least from 25 pages to 15 pages. I think he would do so if there were less stress or tension in the world today. We ourselves have a part in building that tension. We are all individuals in this world, each having individual liberty and each wanting to keep it.
This is why we are fighting for it all the time; but sometimes we forget to use the right methods to go about it. We wait too long and then we have to take up arms to defend our liberties, or to get them back if they have been taken from us. It often happens that somebody oversteps his rights, and when that happens he is necessarily stepping on somebody else's rights. In this area we have a great job to do, not only in Canada and America but across the world. We belong to the Atlantic treaty organization, to NORAD, to the United Nations and other world-wide organizations. I think we had an example not too long ago of how race, colour, religion, nationality, social stature, and so on, need not enter into this question. I refer to the Olympic games that were held in Tokyo. The athletes there came from every nation in the world, including Russia; but there was something that struck me and most of our Canadian sports commentators over there, and this was the link, the understanding among these people.
I will tell you one thing, sir. There was no suggestion of declaring an international war at those Olympic games. They had something in common; they had a common interest; they understood each other. This is the direction in which the United Nations, NATO and NORAD should be moving now. They should be cutting down on arming themselves with nuclear weapons and trying to beat the enemy in manufacturing nuclear weapons. They should get out and try the other course; that is, beating the enemy at giving more information and helping nations to understand each other as much as possible. In that way we would at least be trying to achieve real peace, not by fear but by understanding and comprehension.
The army is needed, and so is the air force and the navy; but not in order to fight wars or defend our own skins. We need them for other things. We need organized forces like these for the purposes of which I spoke previously when the minister presented his white paper. I refer to having an organized, mobile army at home in order that we may use it when needed in order to fight conflagra-20220-624J
Supply-National Defence tion, floods or any kind of emergency that may arise. In that way our forces could help this nation not only in time of war but in peacetime, and they would not have to be shining buttons all the time. It is all right to have discipline; it is all right to have well dressed officers; it is all right to look sharp. I go along with that, but as well as a smart appearance we must deal with urgent needs in this country and in the world. Canada is playing a role in Cyprus today, a peace role. But if we had moved in in time to give these people the opportunity to think about what was happening before they engaged in a quarrel, as they did, and perhaps if we had done our job three years ago in regard to that island, and the United Nations had worked in that way to greater advantage, we would not have Canadian troops standing between the Turks and the Greeks over there. It is all right to be the referee in a matter like this, but I like the rules to be laid down before anything starts.
This is the part I wanted to talk about today, a part that we often forget in this house; in fact, I have not heard it mentioned too often. I do not want hon. members to suppose that I am giving a moral lecture, because I am not. That is not the attitude I am taking and I do not want hon. members to take that point of view. I am putting this forward as something that everyone in this house should be conscious of with regard to national defence or any other activity. It is this. When we do something, we should be doing it for the welfare of the nation. When I talk about the nation I am talking about industry, about companies, about families, about municipalities, about school boards, and about every single individual in this nation; and the nation shall be itself a proud, strong nation as long as the individual stands up proudly and strongly himself. This is very much like the apple cart; the apple cart is worth a lot so long as the apples in it are not rotten. If we do not take time to correct a situation when it begins, soon we will have everybody feeling the effects of some little, cock-eyed idea of a person or group of persons; and these things sometimes cause a national calamity and crisis. We have to guide the nation, to tell the nation what to do. But we have to do it ourselves. We have to tell ourselves what to do and when to do it. That is one thing we should not forget.
I am saying to you, sir, and to the Minister of National Defence that we have a war to fight all right-but not with arms, at the

Supply-National Defence moment. We have wars to fight across the world today. One of the greatest wars is fighting communism. Does the minister expect to fight communism with an atomic bomb? Does he expect to kill with an atomic bomb the idea that communism is better than the free, democratic world in which we live? He does not believe that for one single moment; nobody does. But what are we doing? We are arming ourselves in case somebody from the other side decides to take over this part of the world. But we sit and wait; we do not want to be an aggressor. I know why: It is because deep down in our hearts we know we will not attain any kind of goal by trying to destroy the eastern bloc with arms of any kind. The eastern bloc idea is for communism to creep throughout the world by one method, and it is going to creep into Canada if we let things go that far. They try to spread communism through our own social security, through our own misery at home, through hunger and misunderstanding. This is when they come in with the magic formula. This is how they got into some of the satellite countries of Russia. This is how communism got into Russia itself. This is how it is creeping now into the countries of South America where hunger prevails.
In this connection I would refer to statistics of the last world war. These are not my statistics; our dominion bureau of statistics can give them to you. They were produced by an international bureau of statistics, I imagine, although I do not know where they were picked up from. All I look at are the the figures they give me. They took long enough picking them up, so I am not going back to find out where they came from. With regard to the last world war, more people died in one day from hunger during the world crisis than during the worst week of the war. We fought the war but we forgot to fight this monster that was with us during the last world crisis. There are still signs and pangs of it here today. We sent our Canadian troops over to defend this nation, and they did it proudly. But they wanted to defend something else; they did not want only to defend us from the enemy, or prevent the enemy coming over here. They fought hoping that this country would continue to progress; that this country would be able to give three meals a day to the people living in it. They fought for these ideals, just as Americans did for America and as the English did for England.
I think the Minister of National Defence, who is primarily concerned with this business


of warfare, should give some thought to this. I am sure he has already, but I would ask him to extend his thinking and meditation in this way. If he does I assure him he will have the best army which ever existed either on this continent or anywhere else, on the day we stop thinking in terms of who is stronger in the military field, and start thinking about who is stronger in understanding human beings.
We sometimes forget here the principles with which we were born. Until these principles are restored to their right place, no matter what kind of army or nuclear forces exist they will not be strong enough to appease the uprisings which occur across the world. More and more these uprisings, both in the past as well as today, are caused by hunger and social insecurity, and in many cases by regulations imposed by governments. There is enough in this world for everyone to live on, and it is up to us to distribute these goods to each and every one.
Someone has said that war contributes only to the well-being of those who manufacture or purchase war materials, and I agree with that. As a result of the last world war we were left billions of dollars in debt. A lot of Canadians were literally slaughtered, as was the growing youth of other nations. Who profited from the war? A few more millionaires came into being, but that is all; everybody else is still paying for it. Sometimes we forget that during the ten years preceding the war we needed to look down to each individual's needs and problems of the moment. We have a little insecurity in our own country at the present time. We hear talk of extremism on one side or the other, and of separatism. But if we looked at the heart of the problem we would see we had forgotten something. If this parliament has also forgotten, let it say "Mea culpa" and try and correct the situation as soon as possible.
In my own province there is an area where there is social insecurity now-the closing of a mine with consequent unemployment. Do you think, Mr. Chairman, that these people are worried about how many bombs we have or how many nuclear arms there are on NATO soil? They are more worried about whether they are going to eat tomorrow morning. If they are left in that state we will not be worrying for long about NATO; we will be worrying about the guys who come up to Ottawa and perhaps cause more turmoil than we already have. This is because of the social insecurity there is at home and the economic gaps in the system which fail to provide the

people with the basic requirements, such as a home, security for their children and for their families. That is what they want. I think the government should look at this problem more closely.
I go along with the minister in reducing his defence budget. I congratulate him for this, although he has not reduced many of his activities. However, I hope he reduces his expenses a little more. He has integrated the forces. Let us hope they are all united in one group and that he will direct them to fight for this common problem across the world, the problem of hunger and misery. It is there, do not worry. Two thirds of the people in the world today go to bed at night starving, so something must be wrong. I think it is the responsibility of the government to discover what is wrong, to correct the mistake and to try to bring about a real peace both in our nation and in other nations.
I have referred to this particular aspect today, which has been left aside to a certain axtent in view of the fact that Remembrance day is approaching and has brought back to me memories of the things for which our brothers fought, and possibly that has inspired me to talk on this particular aspect of national defence, our responsibility to this nation and to the world. If the minister has not got any, I have many books I would gladly lend him written by independent authors, writers, businessmen, leaders and nation leaders across the world, past and present, all of them dealing exactly with this subject. So far many governments have turned a deaf ear to this sort of plea, and thus caused international crises, calamities and wars. I think it is the responsibility of the government at least to open its ears and to listen to what nations and the people in them have to say; because when one listens to the social worker, the labourer, the civil servant at the bottom of the ladder, the farmers and their children, the housewife, and so on, and hears their grievances, he can be pretty sure that he has reached the heart of the nation. That is where the strength of a nation lies. That is where the best national defence you could ever hope for lies. Destroy it and you have not even got a country to defend.
That is where I should like the Minister of National Defence to concentrate his efforts, along with those of his colleagues in the cabinet, and give peace of mind first of all to the people who need it, to the people who want it and to the people who are yelling and begging for it. When you do this you
Supply-National Defence will find you have the best national army you could ever want for a country, and it would be the best example we could give to the world to show that we can attain peace economically at home, and by the same means internationally, because the same thing would result if this were done in other countries as well as Canada.

Mr. Chairman, my first general criticism of the minister and the government with regard to defence could be summed up in the phrase that theirs is a record of big talk and small performance. The minister's publicity machine has been working overtime ever since he took office, and as a result the general public has been given the impression that great financial savings were being made and that great things were being accomplished in the way of increasing the efficiency of our defence forces, while ini actual fact expenditures have increased! rather than decreased and our general defence situation has steadily been weakened.
I object on general principles, and I object as far as defence matters are concerned in particular, to this kind of propaganda which gives the people of Canada a false picture of what is going on in matters of defence. It is the sort of thing which I hope the minister will stop. The Canadian people have been led to believe, as a result of statement after statement about savings to be made, that the minister was cutting down the cost of defence and thus making money available for other government purposes; or, perhaps of more interest to them, for making tax cuts.
The last speaker at one point complimented the minister for cutting down defence expenditure. That member is a member of the defence committee but he does not seem to realize that instead of defence expenditures being cut down they have actually been increased. This fact is indicated by a press release which came out only last week, on October 28. A Canadian press article by Dave McIntosh states in part as follows:
Defence spending in the 1963-64 fiscal year rose to its highest point in the last seven years, officials have disclosed.
Despite slashes in some navy and R.C.A.F. equipment programs, defence expenditures in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1964, amounted to $1,683,471,903, the biggest outlay on defence since the $1,759,426,000 spent in 1955-57 when the Liberal government was last in office.
This is a fact of which the general public has not the slightest inkling. I know as a result of some letters I have received and conversations I have had with several indi-

The situation as disclosed by this article was exactly opposite to what they had been led to believe by statements made by the minister about the general situation. They thought the reverse situation was true, and there would be quite a saving which could be applied in the form of tax cuts, or for some other purpose.
The article then continues as follows:
The Liberals, who again assumed power in April, 1963, have promised to reduce expenditures on defence department housekeeping-military personnel costs and operations and maintenance-and increase spending on new weapons in equipment.

This article in the last sentence states:
The original 1963-64 defence estimate approved by parliament was $1,590,006,537. Actual defence expenditures were $93,464,466 higher.
The estimates for 1963-64 were prepared when I was minister, submitted to and received the approval of treasury board. However, the expenditures were made almost entirely during a period when the present minister was in office. He was the person responsible for this increase of some $90 million odd in the expenditures over what we had planned to spend for military purposes last year.
While this increase in expenditures was taking place, as I have said I will demonstrate by what I have to say in the next few minutes, our general military posture was steadily weakening, or decreasing. Before going on to some of those other matters I should like
[Mr. Harkness.j

to state that I am pleased that the white paper and the minister's statement have made it clear that our general defence policy of the past seven, eight or ten years is to be continued. That is, our strong support of NATO, NORAD and the United Nations will continue to be the basis of our defence policy.
The speakers who immediately preceded me, and who sit in the left hand corner of this chamber, have cast considerable doubt on the value of NATO and have advocated in some cases that we should put an end to our NATO expenditures and apparently leave our defence in the hands of the gods. What they do not seem to realize is that no country at the present time can look after its security except through an adherence to a system of alliances. No country, particularly one such as Canada, has adequate resources to look after its own defence entirely alone. The only way in which we can obtain a reasonable amount of protection and security is by combining with like-minded nations, pooling our resources with theirs, from a military point of view, and obtaining the maximum amount of security at a minimum cost. However, we cannot expect other countries of NATO or of the western world to protect us if we are not prepared to pay something for that protection. The idea that we should get a free ride in this regard is one which is not worthy of us as Canadians, and one which is completely irresponsible and pays no attention to what is the general situation in the world today.
There is no doubt that we must continue in our support of these three great alliances, and if we expect them to continue to be effective we must play our reasonable part, and by "reasonable part" I refer to one which is related to our population resources.
In actual fact this is one of our difficulties at the present time. The proportion of our manpower which we devote to military purposes to play our part in these alliances, particularly in the case of NATO, is considerably smaller than that of most of the other members. The proportion of our gross national product which we devote to military purposes for the support of NATO has been steadily decreasing year after year for quite a number of years. The proportion of our actual government expenses devoted to military purposes has been decreasing. Our position in NATO relative to our allies has been getting worse all the time, rather than the reverse.
The main question to be asked is whether we should not really be increasing the proportion of our resources which we devote to

these purposes in order to play our fair part in the defence of the entire west. One of the things I think we must also realize, but which is not realized by quite a number of people, is that our adherence to these alliances determines to a very considerable extent the size and the organization of our defence forces. We have assumed certain responsibilities to NATO, to NORAD and to the United Nations, and in order to meet those responsibilities we have provided and must continue to provide certain types of military forces. Everyone in the house I am sure is familiar with what those are, and I will not go into detail.
I should also like to note that I was pleased to hear the minister state this morning that the nuclear armament has now been supplied for the Bomarc, for some of the 104's, and for the Honest John battery, and that the armament for the 101 aircraft for the defence of Canada is expected to be supplied some time in the new year. This was one of the chief election pledges of the present government. I have been extremely surprised that they have been so slow in implementing it. I find it extremely difficult to understand why it has taken them a year and a half to implement this decision, and yet the 101's are not equipped with nuclear weapons. I believe this is an example of the slowness of the government in getting things done. Having taken the main decision to acquire nuclear weapons for weapons systems which were already in existence, I think the government has been deficient in the lack of speed they have shown in accomplishing that purpose.
Now, this is one case in which the general position of the defence force has been improved. However, in other directions we have been steadily falling behind so far as our commitments to NATO are concerned. I think the minister and most other members of the house are well aware of the fact that we are steadily and rapidly falling behind in the number of naval vessels which we have available or will have available in the years ahead to meet our responsibilities for our own local coastal defence and our commitments to NATO. This is a matter which has been of considerable concern to me because of the time lag between the institution of a naval building program and the time you actually get these ships into service. This time lag in the past has always run between four and five years. I think it is very doubtful whether there will be any improvement in the future. The present government scrapped the general purpose frigate program
Supply-National Defence which had been started, but has substituted nothing for it. The minister did say today that he hoped to be able to make an announcement in a few weeks about some naval rebuilding program. However, there will be a considerable time lag during which we will be deficient in meeting our naval responsibilities.
The same things applies so far as the Canadian air division in Europe is concerned. We had agreed to provide an air division of eight squadrons of CF-104's equipped for the strike-reconnaissance role, which meant nuclear equipment. This government has equipped six of those squadrons with nuclear weapons. The other two squadrons have been converted to the reconnaissance role and are going to be armed with some type of unknown or unspecified conventional weapons. What this means, in effect, is that the actual striking power of the air division has been reduced about 25 per cent, a very material reduction in our obligations to NATO so far as air power is concerned. It is all very well for the minister and his government to talk about meeting our commitments to NATO and other people, and they have to some extent met them as they said they would in regard to supplying some nuclear weapons for the weapons systems we have in Europe, but they have considerably reduced what we had agreed to provide. They are failing in this regard.
Another thing upon which I should like to comment is the closing down of a large number of military installations. Undoubtedly -I think nobody would argue this-this process really weakens our actual and potential military strength. I am quite prepared to agree that in some cases the closing down of these installations was justified in order to save money for expenditures in other lines. However, what I do object to is misrepresenting the situation by saying that the closing down of these military operations has actually improved our military situation. This is what the minister is constantly doing. I feel the minister should quite frankly lay the cards on the table and say, we have closed this installation, that one or the other, in order to save money for some other purpose because the total amount of money we have is limited. I think it is completely wrong to try to pretend that while you are doing this you are increasing your military effectiveness when, as a matter of fact, you are actually decreasing it.

The reorganization of national defence headquarters is a matter upon which I spoke at considerable length when the bill providing the legal basis for that was before us. I do not propose to repeat what I said at that time except to say that, in my opinion, some basic mistakes were made. I refer particularly to the introduction of what has been called the supremo concept, having a single military adviser on whom the minister has to depend for all his military advice. I think the history of military organization in western Europe has shown clearly that this is not as good a system as the one we had, whereby you had a chief of staff for each service. I believe our future experience will show that this is the case.
I should like to say of course, and I think no one realizes it better than I do, that some reorganization was required at national defence headquarters. Parkinson's law had been at work there for many years, and certainly a reorganization was required. The present minister may recall that as long ago as when I was before in opposition, I used to be pointing out that this was a necessity, and pointing to some of the overgrown staffs, branches and what not. I might say that while I was minister I started on this process, as the minister is aware, by setting up a ministerial manpower commission whose job it was to survey the entire personnel set-up of national defence headquarters and to recommend how that could be reduced or reorganized. I have no doubt that perhaps a considerable amount of the work of that commission has proven useful in the reorganization which is going on there now. So far as the reorganization of national defence headquarters is concerned, I quite agree some reorganization was required. I do express reservations as to the way in which the reorganization is being carried out so far as some phases of it are concerned.
In so far as this matter of integration of the services is concerned, it has been quite apparent ever since the minister made his first statement in regard to the matter that there was no plan in existence so far as integration below national defence headquarters was concerned. This long delay in issuing a statement on what will happen below the level of national headquarters in Ottawa has given rise to a great deal of uncertainty on the part of serving personnel. There is nothing which produces decline of morale more rapidly than uncertainty, and it is extremely unfortunate there has been such a


long delay, with still no prospect of a statement being made.
This morning the minister said that stage two, the next step, would be integration of commands. However, he gave no indication what the term "integration of commands" means. If he has any plan with regard to it, then surely this is the place and now is the time to make it known, so that members of the committee may have an opportunity to express their opinions on it.
Neither has the defence committee been told what is to be done below the level of national defence headquarters. If there is any plan dealing with integration below the Ottawa level the time is long past when it should have been disclosed to hon. members.
From some of the statements made in recent months by the minister and the associate minister, I gather that what seemed to be the minister's original idea of rolling all the services into one bale or one pot, if it may be described that way, has now been seen to be an impractical and impossible proposition. You just cannot move a man from an army job to a naval or air force job, and I hope the minister now has firmly in his mind the fact that fighting units cannot be disturbed very much. They have to remain pretty well as they are. It is just an impossibility to switch an infantry officer to fly a jet plane, or anything else along that line.
I would like to hear what is planned concerning integration of the administrative services. There is no doubt this is the area in which integration can be carried forward with resultant considerable savings and, I would hope, an improvement in efficiency. I would urge the minister to make a statement on this matter.
Once more this morning the minister tried to give the impression, when speaking on equipment, that these were all new programs which he and the present government had instituted, and that the improvement which would result from them would be entirely due to this government. In actual fact in all cases they were programs which were instituted whilst the Conservative government was in office.
Dealing first with armoured personnel carriers, the minister is well aware that we had a program to produce these in Canada, but unfortunately it did not proceed as rapidly as everyone hoped it would. He scrapped that program and purchased armoured personnel carriers from the United States, and I have

no quarrel with that. In fact I am glad the personnel carriers will be delivered soon.
Heavy helicopters for the army were ordered and were in the course of production long before the minister assumed office, and the fact is that they are just now coming into service. The same situation applies to the anti-tank missile.
So far as the navy is concerned, the program to equip destroyer escorts with variable depth sonar was well under way before I ceased to be minister of national defence. Similarly, plans for the Oberon class submarine were advanced to the stage where they were just waiting for a final arrangement between the British government and ourselves which would involve the British buying some equipment from us. Research on a hydrofoil vessel and the production of a prototype had also been launched. There is nothing new in any of these things. We purchased four of the Hercules aircraft to see how they would work out, and if satisfactory said we would purchase more. They did prove satisfactory and now the program is proceeding.
I was glad to hear the minister say that the NORAD agreement will be renewed, thus setting at rest rumours which have been current in newspaper articles that it would not be renewed. I thoroughly agree with him that it is essential for us to play our part in this agreement for the joint defence of the North American continent.
The minister also said today that he hoped within a few weeks to be able to announce a shipbuilding program. Last week the associate minister made a statement which seemed to indicate that what is planned is some type of troop carrying vessel. If they are planning to build naval vessels which would have the primary function of transporting army personnel I hope that plan will not be proceeded with, because there could be no greater waste of naval funds than to build ships of that kind. Ordinary merchant vessels are available in large numbers and can always be secured in order to transport personnel whenever such a requirement arises.
Basically our navy has primarily been an antisubmarine navy, and its continuance in that role is confirmed by statements in the white paper. Therefore I hope the type of ship to be built will contribute toward that role, or if the role is to be changed we should be told so at this time instead of waiting until an announcement is made on the type of ship to be built, a type that might not contribute much to naval effectiveness even
Supply-National Defence though it would provide some work for our shipyards.
If what the associate minister had in mind was a type of naval aircraft carrier which could be adopted for carrying personnel, tanks and other equipment, and which could be used for various task force purposes, then this means a departure in the general policy which has been pursued so far as the navy is concerned, and we should be given an opportunity of discussing that.
I would like to say something about the reserve forces but I see my time is practically at an end, so I shall resume my chair and come back to that matter later.

speechtext:
My remarks on
these estimates will be brief. It is not my intention to be repetitive, and therefore I shall not attempt to deal with subjects already dealt with by the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Edmonton West. However, I do want to ask the minister for a further explanation of his observations with regard to the integration program. I should like him to give, once and for all, a definition of what he means by integration. I should like him to say how far the program of integration is to go within the definition he gives. He did say that the unification of headquarters was in progress, that stage two would be the integration of commands and stage three the integration of schools. As I recall it, he stopped at that point. Are we to assume that this is the total picture, or are there to be stages four, five, six, and seven and so on which he did not mention, but which nevertheless he has in mind? If he does have further stages in mind, what are these stages? I believe the members of the various services are not completely sure what the future policy may be in this regard.
The minister mentioned savings which might accrue as a result of integration but, as has already been said, the term "savings" in this context is inaccurate. What the minister may have in mind is a direction of defence spending along different channels, with increased accent on certain types of expenditure and a reduction in other fields. I have no quarrel with this as long as it can be justified. But something which has been completely omitted from the minister's remarks is a reference to the cost of this reorganization. It is well and good to give the picture on one side of the coin only, but we must also have an idea of what this reorganization is costing in terms of extra expense having to
9864	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence do with the premature retirement of personnel, and so on. More important still is the cost in terms of the effort which is being expended at the present time on this reorganization and I should like to have some estimate of this cost if one has been made. I presume that at the present time a large number of personnel of all ranks are devoting a large part of their time, if not all of their time, to the solution of the problems caused by reorganization itself. This has to be placed on one side of the balance against the gains which are visualized on the other, because it is only net savings in which we are interested. If we were starting from scratch to set up a department of national defence and defence services, one system might have a considerable advantage over another. But it does not necessarily follow that there is any advantage in changing from one system to another. It is like remodelling the floor plan of a house; the cost may be greater than the advantages, or at least the cost has to be subtracted from the advantages gained.
The minister could not be expected to cover all the aspects of defence in the limited time available to him, but he omitted to mention in his remarks what progress has been made in the study which a special committee on antisubmarine warfare has been conducting. I may not have called the committee by its correct name, but I have a special interest in this subject; the committee is conducting a study of the proper mix of aircraft and naval units for the most effective conduct of antisubmarine warfare and coastal defence.

speechtext: I referred to that in my statement.

speechtext:
Only briefly; but I should like to have a fuller statement as to what changes in policy are contemplated as a result of this study. If there are changes involved I should also like to know whether the minister is in a position to spell them out accurately and in detail, and perhaps he would tell us at what point they will come into effect.
I intend to say a word now about a recent announcement of decisions by the department of defence with regard to the closing down of reserve units. As is generally known, committees were appointed, one for the air force, one for the navy and one for the army, to study the position of the reserve units in all three categories. In most cases the department accepted the recommendations of these committees though, of course, not in all cases.


I think it is unfortunate that the department did not see fit to accept the recommendation of the Hendy committee that H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte, which happens to be in my constituency, should be continued. I am perhaps being parochial up to a point, but I say this because of wider interests. I think it is an unfortunate anomaly that our small province of Prince Edward Island should be the only province in Canada without any naval presence whatever, as will be the case when this unit is closed.
The unit has been in existence for about 40 years. It has an excellent record, and in this connection I might say that all the reserve units in Prince Edward Island have always received magnificent support from the general population. As a matter of fact, on a per capita basis, compared with the country as a whole the number of people who have over the years entered the militia and the other reserve units is about three times as great as the national average. I admit at once of course that there are areas in Canada where the opportunity to join the reserve forces is not as great. However, this particular reserve force had a magnificent record during the last war. I cannot quote this as an accurate figure but I believe more than 150 naval officers who had been members of the Queen Charlotte before world war II or in the early days of world war II served in the Canadian navy during that war. This is a magnificent contribution to the war effort to come from such a small unit as this, and I believe it is unfortunate that the unit has been done away with.
I have an uneasy feeling that when the Hendy committee was appointed to deal with this subject the public was told that it had been appointed to give advice to the department as to how the money spent on these units could be used to the best advantage so that as many as possible should be kept in existence. However, the fact seems to be that the committee was actually formed so as to give these reserve navy units a decent burial, as it were. To continue the analogy, the people who thought they were being called in as medical advisers found that their duties were actually those of pallbearers. In the Hendy report I find this statement on page 27:
While no official decision on this will be reached until-
He is speaking of the naval reserve divisions:
-the report of the militia commission is completed it is certainly obvious that the militia are looking forward to the acquisition and use

of the buildings which the naval divisions have been directed to surrender.
Yet the government was trying to create the impression that no final decision had yet been taken and these reports were being asked for in good faith. The Hendy committee had this to say about H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte, and I will quote briefly:
This division located in a provincial capital and on salt water would be expected to have naval facilities established in emergency. The division is admirably located overlooking the harbour with communication facilities. It is not, however, using its building anywhere near to maximum use for defence purposes... .It is believed the militia also wish to acquire this building and it would seem that some space sharing arrangement is feasible here as in other centres. This will, of course, have to await findings of the militia commission. As the division will not be closed until December first of this year, it would seem that there would be no problem in entering into consultation and making concrete proposals at a later date, but it is certainly the committee's recommendation that every effort be made to retain this division because of its particular situation although a complement probably not more than 15 officers, 50 men and 10 Wrens is indicated and this should be borne in mind in determining the utilization and allocation of costs between the various users.
However, when the commission on the reorganization of the army reported, the report indicated that it contemplated having all the militia units that were to survive in Charlottetown housed in H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte. I can only draw two conclusions from this: Either the army reorganization committee knew beforehand that the government was going to close down Queen Charlotte and therefore it was available to them, or there is still room in H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte for the naval reserve unit as well as a militia unit. If that is the case, the justification for closing down H.M.C.S. Queen Charlotte is reduced. The explanation that was given the other day in committee seemed to be that this was just a question of mind-reading; one did not happen to know what the other was doing and it was a case of serendipity and just happened this way. This, in my mind, does not quite wash. I do not want to say any more about that, Mr. Chairman. I have lodged my statement of non-approval of what has been done in this connection, and I believe I am not alone in this respect, because this view is shared not only by the people who are interested in the naval reserve as such but by the general population of Prince Edward Island. With regard to the militia reorganization, I have no particular quarrel with the reorganization as it affects my own constituency or Prince Edward Island generally. I think it was recognized that these are on the
Supply-National Defence whole excellent units and there was a minimum of reduction in the establishment there. I want to express my appreciation of that fact.
However, in the wider view I think it is unfortunate-the minister may wonder why I have any particular interest in this, but I did live in Vancouver for a year on one occasion-that the recommendation of the militia commission with regard to the Irish Fusiliers in Vancouver was not accepted. I say this because, perhaps only by coincidence, the Irish regiment in Toronto is also one of the units which got the chop, and I believe there are two other cases of units which have an historic association with some particular groups of citizens or people of some particular racial origin, at least technically. I think it is unfortunate that two of the Irish units in Canada should be wiped out at the same time. It is true that they have only nominally been disbanded. What has happened to them is that they have been transferred to the supplementary order of battle, which is a polite way of saying that they are going to be sort of embalmed to give the impression that they are still alive-the same idea as Lenin's tomb in Moscow, or something of this sort.
As far as I can read this, it has no significance whatsoever except that these units will probably be represented by some dead files in a filing cabinet somewhere in headquarters and perhaps they will have the honour of having their colours deposited in a church somewhere, and their silverware and this sort of thing may still be retained in the armouries they originally occupied. But as far as I can see, as units it is just a figure of speech to say they have been transferred to the supplementary order of battle. They just do not exist-unless it means that if at some future date there should be an expansion of the militia, these units would have priority with regard to being revived. If that is the case, it makes a little bit of sense and there is some shred of consolation for the people who are particularly interested in them.
I would like the minister to clarify that small point. I would have hoped there would be a little more awareness of the fact that these reserve units have a special meaning to the civilian population who have served in them from time to time. This may be brushed aside as foolish sentiment; but it is well to remember that the greatest military exploits of all time and the finest units in all armies of all time had this bit of sentiment, which meant the difference between being just a good,

Supply-National Defence efficient unit and a superb one. That is all I have to say at the moment, Mr. Chairman.
