speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there will not be time for me to complete my remarks today in just the 20 minutes remaining, but I can make a start on them. I echo the disappointment my colleagues have mentioned in regard to the statement made by the minister today. My seatmate, the hon. member for Queens, was just too charitable; he said it was unfortunate that the minister did not have more time to complete his statement. On the introduction of estimates the committee has never refused an extension of time to ministers making statements with regard to their departments; so the minister was not limited to 30 minutes. In fact, he should have gone on, and the committee would have welcomed a complete, comprehensive statement with regard to the policy of the Department of National Defence, with regard to the efficiency of the forces at the present time, with regard to our commitments overseas and with regard to the most recent announcement concerning the reorganization of the Canadian militia.
I said at the conclusion of his remarks that it was a shocking omission not to say something today about the proposed reorganization of the Canadian militia, and I will deal with that on the next occasion these estimates come before us. Because to omit any reference today, when the minister's estimates are before the committee for the first time in this calendar year, to the Canadian militia, who received a very severe blow within the last week, is inexcusable. There was not one word of thanks from the Minister of National Defence to the militia, who have served this country from its origin and who are serving the country at the present time. No ray of hope was given to those who are in doubt today as to what may be their future. That is an attitude on the part of the Minister of National Defence that cannot be excused, and I hope that some of my colleagues will deal at length with that subject in the future.
When the former minister of national defence, the hon. member for Calgary North, was speaking a few minutes ago he drew attention to the sham surrounding the present Minister of National Defence and his department. He mentioned the fact-we have drawn attention to this matter before but I reiterate it-that we have had a great press personal relations build-up of an incompetent Minister of National Defence. We have had statements on the radio and on television and


press stories about what this man was to do. But what have been the accomplishments in the year and a half in which this minister has been in office? There has been a great ballyhoo across the country about the savings which were going to be made. As the hon. member for Calgary North pointed out, the expenditure in the last fiscal year was the highest for seven years. What saving has been effected in the fiscal year 1963-64? What saving is going to be effected in the fiscal year 1964-65? The estimates placed before us -the main estimates plus a supplementary estimate-indicate that on the basis of the very large figures for the preceding fiscal year there will be a saving of $100 million odd. I suggest that by the time further supplementary estimates have reached us, either this month, next month or in January, February or March, there will be an even higher expenditure in the Department of National Defence than in the last fiscal year.
How is the minister to live up to his promises unless there is more money available? This pretence that he is saving money by chopping off militia units, closing down establishments, retiring officers of long service on three months' notice and reducing the total strength of our forces represents no effective saving which has been shown to us today; it is only a transfer of expenditure from one area to another.
The minister told us a year and a half ago when explaining this matter to us in the house-he repeated it when we had the white paper in front of us and then when we had the bill setting up his supremo-that unless something were done immediately the amount of money available for replacement of equipment for the navy, army and air force would not be forthcoming but that all the money would be utilized to pay the personnel who are in the services plus the housekeeping charges. We are fully aware of that; there was to be a decrease in the amount of money available for equipment. But the minister has tried to mislead the Canadian people to the extent that he was going to make such savings on housekeeping, on streamlining the forces and increasing efficiency-these are some of his own words-that he would have money available for equipment.
About a year and a half ago he reported in one of these magnificent press releases that he was entering upon a 60 day period of decision during which he was going to place orders for equipment for the navy, the army and the air force. He is still fiddling around with this. Where are these orders

for new equipment for the services? Except for certain transport planes and for armoured personnel carriers and anti-tank weapons there has been none. What about the navy? What are we going to do about the air force, with the long range policy which is planned for it? In wartime we used to have a branch of the army known as the camouflage branch. The minister should be colonel in chief of a reactivated camouflage branch of the Department of National Defence, because I say that this matter has been camouflaged. He has pretended to the Canadian people that enormous savings were being made without decrease in efficiency, when this has not in fact resulted. I question very much, as did the hon. member for Calgary North, whether the efficiency of our fighting forces has been maintained.
Now, Mr. Chairman, let me indicate some of the deception to which we have been subjected over these last two years. It is just about two years since the Minister of National Defence and the present Prime Minister were talking in this house about defence policy and what they were going to do when they got into office. All you have to do, Mr. Chairman, is to look back to the session of 1962-63, where you will find some of the statements made by these gentlemen at that time. I wonder whether the Minister of National Defence thinks as much of his vaunted Bomarcs now as he did two years ago. Two years ago, or almost two years ago-February 4, 1963-he said, as reported at page 3429 of Hansard:
Mr. McNamara has not much more faith in it than I have.
That was in speaking of the Bomarc. Almost two years ago he had no faith in the Bomarcs. Now he has equipped them with nuclear weapons. What faith has he got in them at the present time? They are sitting ducks for the first missile to attack this continent in the event of nuclear war. I asked the minister several questions during the course of the last two or three months about the arming of our forces. I asked him whether nuclear missiles had been provided for the Honest John battery in Europe; whether the 104 air division over there had nuclear missiles; whether the Voodoo planes in Canada had nuclear missiles. All these things were going to be attended to. They told us that these matters should have been done by February, 1963. They said we were not living up to our commitments and that these missiles and nuclear devices were to be supplied. To the questions which I asked the min-
Supply-National Defence ister, his reply in the summer was that they had not been supplied or that he did not know whether they had. It is only recently that he has informed us that the Honest John battery in Europe may now be provided with nuclear missiles. Why were they not provided when this minister took office in April, 1963? If we were in default, and those are the words he used in February, 1963, the present government stayed in default until just a few weeks ago.
What about the nuclear weapons for the 104's in Europe? Have nuclear weapons been supplied to that great air division? I asked the minister that question some time ago and his explanation was that the air division was operative. He did not say it had nuclear missiles. I wanted to know whether the aircraft of that division were on alert stations with nuclear weapons attached to the aircraft. He just said the air division was operative. Perhaps he will answer that question now. Are nuclear weapons available for our air squadron in Germany? Are some of the aircraft sitting at action alert with nuclear bombs attached to their fuselages? The minister does not answer my questions. All we are told is that the air division is operative.
I asked him a question about the two squadrons in France which are not armed with nuclear weapons or with conventional weapons. His answer was that the photographic equipment used by those squadrons constituted armament. I do not know what sort of a missile or bullet could be fired from a camera, but that was his answer. He said we were in default in respect of our alleged commitments, when speaking in this house in February, 1963. He had been over to Europe and was talking about the nuclear equipment of the air division and said, as reported at page 3427 of Hansard:
We were also told that the first squadron was intended to go on target on May 1, 1963 and that in order to go on target a bilateral agreement would have to be signed with the United States by November 1-
That was November 1, 1962. Then he continued as follows:
-NATO headquarters in Europe puts a very high priority on that particular project. The infrastructure, as it is called, the runway extensions and the ammunition depots to contain these weapons were being built under top NATO priority. It was being considered by the supreme commander and his associates to be an urgent matter because it was recognized that Canada, at the time we were there in November, was in default.
That reference is also November, 1962.

Supply-National Defence
The minister then went on to state:
Well, if we were in default then we are that much more in default at the present time.
The minister made those statements on February 4, 1963. I state to the minister that we were in worse default from the time he took office in April, 1963 until just a few weeks ago than at any time when we had the responsibility for our NATO commitments.
The present minister retired the Sabre jets from the air division in Europe before the 104's had been completely delivered, ready for operations, and before missiles were provided. For almost one year the air division in Europe could not even fire a peanut; it had no weapons at all. That is not the proper action of a responsible minister of defence. We have yet to receive the requested information in this regard.
I have mentioned this situation before, but what I say very frequently does not get the same attention given to statements of the Minister of National Defence and the minister of external affairs. I remember very well that in November and December of 1962, as well as January, 1963, great pictures and stories appeared in the newspapers with headings such as "Honest John Battery in Europe Unarmed''; "104 Aircraft in Europe Unarmed"; "Voodoo Planes in Canada Unarmed".
Canada's defence situation was indicated to the Canadian people as being absolutely incomplete, yet for a space of almost one year the air division in Europe, presently equipped with 104 aircraft, had no weapons to discharge. Did any of you see in the newspapers of this country, the weekly and other magazines, stories about the unarmed air division in Europe?
What about the Voodoo aircraft in Canada? They have not been armed yet with the nuclear missiles about which this minister complained so much when he was sitting on this side of the house. These aircraft were to be equipped immediately for the protection of Canada. In the event there was an air attack we would be caught without missiles on the Bomarc and our Voodoos would not be able to intercept because they were not armed with the required missiles. A period of 18 months has elapsed since this minister took office, yet the Voodoos are still unarmed so far as nuclear missiles are concerned, which he said were so essential to the protection of Canada.


What is the situation in Toronto and Montreal, where the newspapers which carried those headings about unprotected cities were published? The stories suggested that the cities were unprotected because the Conservative government failed to arm the Voodoos with nuclear missiles. Those cities have been unprotected since and are unprotected at this moment.
It being five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, this is perhaps a good time to resume my seat.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. F. Whelan (Essex South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DUTIES OF SPEAKER AFTER DISSOLUTION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-62, to amend the House of Commons Act (Speaker on dissolution).
He said: Mr. Speaker, after having come into this house as a member of the opposition in 1962, and then after having come back into the house after the election in 1963 as a member of the government party-

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DUTIES OF SPEAKER AFTER DISSOLUTION
speechtext: Does that make a difference?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DUTIES OF SPEAKER AFTER DISSOLUTION
speechtext:
It does in this party-I was amazed to find out how this institution we call parliament was run. One of the things that amazed me was the power of the Speaker. It is a constitutional principle of our form of government that a Speaker of the house lives and dies with the house. This principle is incorporated in section 44 of the British North America Act which provides:
The House of Commons on its first assembling after a general election shall proceed with all practicable speed to elect one of its members to be Speaker.
In these few words, there are three constitutional conventions which are as follows:
1.	There can be no Speaker during a dissolution and this vacancy continues until the newly elected House of Commons first assembles;
2.	The house, when it first assembles after a general election, cannot exercise any of its rights, prerogatives, privileges, jurisdictions and duties which are normally in the trusteeship of the Speaker except one, the right to elect the Speaker;

3.	The Speakership dies when the house is dissolved because the Speaker must be a member, and when the house dissolves there are no members.
Except by amending our constitution, we cannot depart from the principle that there is no Speaker of the house during a dissolution of parliament. This is so because section 18 of the British North America Act provides:
The privileges, immunities, and powers to be held, enjoyed and exercised by the Senate and by the House of Commons, and by the members thereof respectively, shall be such as are from time to time defined by act of the parliament of Canada, but so that any act of the parliament of Canada defining such privileges, immunities, and powers shall not confer any privileges, immunities, or powers, exceeding those at the passing of such act held, enjoyed, and exercised by the commons house of parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and by the members thereof.
When we refer to the constitutional position in the United Kingdom, which we cannot exceed, we find that in 1704 the house of lords and the house of commons jointly agreed as follows:
That neither house of parliament have power, by any vote or declaration, to create to themselves new privileges, not warranted by the known laws and customs of parliament.
In the light of these authorities, it is not constitutional for our Speaker to continue as Speaker during dissolution. The constitutional position of the Speaker is recognized in section 15 of the House of Commons Act. This section provides:
The person who fills the office of Speaker at the time of any dissolution of parliament shall, for the purpose of the following provisions of this act, be deemed to be the Speaker until a Speaker is chosen by the new parliament.
The person who is designated in this manner is authorized to prepare and sign the house estimates and to deal with misconduct or unfitness of employees. It is obvious that these powers are only the barest minimum necessary to keep the internal economy of the house functioning. It is obvious also that the person so designated is deemed to be Speaker only for the purpose of status in signing the estimates prepared by the Clerk of the House and Sergeant-at-Arms. The power of disciplining employees is that held by any deputy minister of a department, in this case the Clerk of the House.
There are other statutes which name the Speaker and in which it is not clear whether, constitutionally, they can apply to the Speaker during a dissolution. For example, I cite section 10 of the House of Commons Act respecting a vacancy after a general election;
House of Commons Act the Controverted Elections Act, the Library of Parliament Act, and others.
In 1936 the question of the status of a Speaker, so-called, during a dissolution was referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections. The reference was moved by Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King on March 23, 1936, in the following terms:
That the standing committee on privileges and elections be instructed to inquire into, study and report on, the usages, customs and practices respecting the status of the Speaker of the House of Commons during the period of time which may elapse between any dissolution of the House of Commons and the assembly of a new parliament, and in particular the rights, prerogatives, privileges, jurisdiction and duties ordinarily and customarily exercised by the Speaker under such circumstances in previous years in Canada;
And, also, the status of clerks, officers, messengers or other persons attendant on the House of Commons, distinguishing between such persons as are permanent officers and such as are temporary and those whose duties are of a sessional character;
And the right and proper procedure to be adopted with respect to the retention or dismissal of any such employees;
And that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day, as may be ordered by the committee for the use of the committee and members of the house.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, this reference was made to the standing committee on privileges and elections as a result of the action of the Speaker in dismissing some employees before a new Speaker had been appointed. One of the main reasons for drafting this bill was, as I said, some of the things I learned after coming back into parliament in 1963. Before the session opened that year I was in my office in the west block and, to my amazement, I heard some strange noises in the hall. I wondered who was making these noises. These noises were made by a former minister of the crown and the former Speaker, which I thought was rather strange at the time. The Speaker was checking on the offices, who was in them, how long they had been in these offices, and so on. I asked him what he was doing, and he said he was still the Speaker of the house and still had these powers. I wondered at that time how a person could be appointed a minister of the crown and still be the Speaker of the house, a position that is held in high regard and beyond patronage and political influence. I wondered how a person could be the Speaker, then a minister of the crown, and then go back to being the Speaker. This is why I feel that when the house is dissolved this responsibility should go to the Clerk of the House in whom we have the utmost confidence, and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is rather an odd bill and I hope I will not be considered a little too equivocal in regard to it. I think it is a good idea to bring it forward, but I certainly do not agree with the hon. member and I think a lot of the premises on which he has founded his arguments fall to the ground.
For the purposes of historical accuracy I might inform him that the reference to the committee of the duties of the Speaker did not come about as a result of the actions of the Speaker who was then carrying on, but as a result of the actions of the man who ultimately was to become Speaker, he having moved into the House of Commons a week or ten days before being elected to office and summarily fired some 129 people who were on the staff.
I can also tell the hon. gentleman that if he reads enough of the 1935 Hansard he will find that on the occasion of the election of the Speaker both the prime minister, Mr. King, and the leader of the opposition, Mr. Bennett, gave some very good definitions and descriptions of the office of Speaker, and I would commend them to the hon. member for his edification. It is a matter of historical record that the election of the Speaker of the day was unopposed, on a recorded vote, on condition that the matter be referred to a committee. May I also say that though the election was recorded on division, something which is rather strange, the persons involved were restored to the staff and some of them are still members of the staff.
I think it was unfortunate that the continuing Speaker of the day did not stand by the authority that was granted to him by the act because there would not have been all that difficulty or, shall we say, degradation of the office by another man who had been a member of the house for a considerable length of time and who decided he was going to wield a very heavy patronage axe. Therefore if the hon. member is using the incident of 1935 in order to buttress his arguments, the complete contrary is the result.
I would suggest that one of the strongest arguments is that this is one of those areas in which there should be no vacuum. Again, however, I quarrel with the language of the bill because the hon. member limits it to the Senate and the House of Commons Act, and the requirements of the Financial Ad-


ministration Act must be taken into account. The Speaker is the only person authorized to sign the estimates and confirm certain appointments to the staff.
There is nothing incongruous in the Speaker's continuing in office. After all, a minister continues in office even though he ceases to be a member. So far as the house is concerned the Speaker is in the equivalent position of a minister, and there is nothing that says a minister must be a member of the house, although he cannot take his seat in it unless he be a member.
The hon. member may not be aware that in 1962 the Speaker of the house, the former member for St. Paul's, was defeated in the election, yet he administered the affairs of the house until the very day that I was elected Speaker. Thank goodness he did. I do not know if the hon. member some day aspires to that office, but may I assure him that having the counsel and advice of a continuing Speaker in office is of the greatest importance to a new Speaker.
Another incident that the hon. gentleman has missed occurred in 1953 when Mr. Speaker Macdonald, on dissolution of parliament, was appointed to the other place and appointed solicitor general, yet he continued as Speaker and carried out the functions of that office. May I also inform the hon. gentleman that the position I found myself in, in 1963, was referred for opinion to the law officers of the crown and it was found to be perfectly regular with no disability on my part. As a matter of fact, parliament having been dissolved there was nothing to prevent my taking the position of a minister of the crown without resigning the position of Speaker, because the position had fallen vacant, saving and excepting for the purposes of section 15 and also the requirements of the Financial Administration Act. Certainly the affairs of the house had to be administered by a member, and the person who carries out those functions is a member of the house.

speechtext:
He is a member of the house. He is the man who is carrying on. This is not something that existed only in 1963. It existed in 1962, in 1957, in 1953 and in 1949. In 1945, Mr. Speaker Glen went into the ministry and in 1949, when parliament resumed, Mr. Speaker Fauteux took his seat as an ordinary member until he was appointed to the office of lieutenant governor a matter of a few months after returning to

parliament. But he did act in that period between the dissolution of parliament and the election of Mr. Speaker Macdonald in 1949 or early in 1950.
I have no precise knowledge of what happens in the United Kingdom but I would be the most surprised man in the world if there the clerk were to become speaker pro tern. At no time do we consider an administrator or a deputy minister as eligible to take on the duties of a minister, certainly, within the statutes which parliament has determined. He may, of course, make certain decisions, but under the terms of the Financial Administration Act he would have no power to sign documents, which can only be signed by a minister or an acting minister. This is why we have acting ministers-so that there may be someone who can act at ministerial level. Again, with the Clerk of the House in the chair, I feel that when we come to the election of a Speaker there is a neat point about rulings at that time. The Clerk of the House simply presides in a silent way during the election of Mr. Speaker. He is not the presiding officer of this house. All he does is to read out the letter summoning hon. members to the bar of the other house to attend upon the deputy of His Excellency in order that they may receive instructions from him to elect themselves a Speaker. Then the Clerk of the House is merely in the position of indicating to hon. members that they may have the floor if they wish to propose candidates for the office. Beyond that, the Clerk has no power in this house. He is not in a position to make any decision affecting the members and I would say that in my opinion we would be placing the Clerk of the House as such in a most invidious position were he elevated to a position of authority and protocol as far as the Speakership is concerned.
As I say, there have been other proposals from time to time that there should be a permanent Speaker of this house-that he should be a kind of supra-official, not a member of the house. That is in the same category. But if we stick to the principle that Mr. Speaker should be a member of this house, then I put it to hon. members that it is the Speaker who was in the chair at the time of the dissolution of parliament who should continue to fill the office until a new Speaker has been elected by the house.
As far as the ministry is concerned, again, for the purposes of the Financial Administration Act, if unfortunately there should be a decease or a resignation, a vacation of office for some such reason, then an acting minister
House of Commons Act takes over, not a deputy minister. I put it to hon. members that this practice should continue and I think it is far better for the administration of the affairs of this country that Mr. Speaker who occupied the chair at the time of dissolution should continue to discharge the duties of that office which it is necessary for him to discharge. With all due respect to the Clerk of the House, he is not Mr. Speaker, and therefore Mr. Speaker should continue in office until he is replaced.
After all, there is always a possibility that Mr. Speaker will be re-elected. This happens usually if the administration continues. There is nothing to bar him even if there is a change, though we know of the practical difficulties which may arise. It does happen. In 1957-58 it would have been ludicrous to have Mr. Speaker Michener stand down for all purposes and then come back immediately the new parliament was re-opened in May, 1958 to be re-elected. The same applied to Mr. Speaker Lemieux who carried on for more than one parliament.
So, with the greatest of respect to the hon. member who has put forward this idea, I think that for a multitude of reasons it would be preferable on balance to continue the present arrangement. Since the burden of showing the desirability of change is upon the hon. member who is proposing a change to the house, I suggest the hon. member has failed to discharge that burden, the reasons he has advanced being insufficient.

Certainly I would want some opportunity to discuss this with the present Clerk before we impose such a duty on him. As the hon. member for Edmonton West said, there is some relationship between the situation here, where we have a Speaker and a Clerk, and the depart-


ments of government, where we have a minister and a deputy minister. No one would suggest that in the absence of a minister for any reason whatsoever, the deputy minister should become the minister. House of Commons Act this matter in one hour and delve into all the details of the problems and the possible solutions without having the matter referred to a committee where we can call witnesses for advice.
I think Bill No. C-62 does, in its intentions, tidy up some anomalies perhaps in the official position of Speaker during dissolution, and certainly we should be concerned about it. I should say, also, that some consideration is being given to taking care of the anomalies that we have and the contradictions in the law. For example, the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) quite properly pointed out that under the British North America Act the House of Commons shall appoint or elect one of its members to be the Speaker. There is a contradiction here. All of us know that as of dissolution there are no members of the House of Commons. Therefore if the Speaker must be a member of the house there appears to be some contradiction.
It has been argued that ministers of the crown carry on after dissolution; but it has also been pointed out that ministers of the crown do not have to be members of the House of Commons. Therefore I do not believe that this parallel takes care of the situation. I do not believe in many other respects that there are differences between the position of Speaker, so far as one administering what may be termed the legislative branch of government, and that of a minister of a department, although they are not quite the same.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) contended that he checked with the law officers of the crown during that period between dissolution and the next session of parliament to make sure that he did in fact have the authority to carry on the duties of Speaker. However, I think the reason the law officers gave him that opinion was that there was nothing else for them to do. There is no other provision to provide for the carrying on as head of the legislative branch of parliament during such a period.
I do want to be very brief, Mr. Speaker, in regard to this bill. I think there is some merit in transferring this authority to the Clerk of the House of Commons during dissolution of parliament. At the same time I see some problems arising therefrom, because if you read the bill carefully you will find it provides that:
The Clerk of the House of Commons at the time of any dissolution of parliament shall, for the purposes of this act, be deemed to be the Speaker until a Speaker is chosen by the new parliament.

House of Commons Act
I believe there may be some validity to the argument that the Clerk of the House should carry on some of the administrative duties of the Speaker, but I think those duties should be considerably restricted and by no means amount to the total authority of a Speaker during dissolution.
This brings up the thought, of course, which many of us have held for a long time, namely that there be a permanent Speaker. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated, and I agree, that no member of parliament has ever advocated that a Speaker should continue to hold office on a permanent basis without being re-elected from one parliament to another. This bill specifically deals with that period between parliaments; it does not deal with the period between sessions of the same parliament. So that even if this house did take action to elect a permanent Speaker for an entire parliament, it would still not take care of the period from the date of dissolution of one parliament to the assembly of a new parliament.
I do not want to take up any more time because other hon. members want to speak to this bill, particularly in view of the fact that an amendment has been moved to send its subject matter to a committee. But I do urge all hon. members to support the sending of the subject matter of this bill to a committee because, after all, the committee on procedure and organization has under consideration the Speakership of this house. It is well known to members of the house that there have been some changes in the administrative staff under Mr. Speaker during the past few months. I do not think we should consider those changes as being a complete revision of the administrative staff set-up of this house and which is under the Speaker. This is another of those anomalies which needs to be tidied up, and certainly this should be done before any committee considers the matter and witnesses are called before it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DUTIES OF SPEAKER AFTER DISSOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before the house an amendment to the House of Commons Act to change the status of the Speaker of the House of Commons in order to confer some of the responsibilities which he now exercises upon the Clerk of the House. I may say that in my view this is a very sound proposition and well worth consideration. I say that because of the circumstances which occurred after the end of the election in 1963


and in view of some of the incidents which arose at that time.
Other hon. members have pointed out to the house the responsibilities which rest upon the Speaker when the house is not in session and even when there is no parliament in existence. He has the responsibility of surveying in an administrative way the functioning of the house. He also has other very important responsibilities. However, I suggest in this connection, as in all other connections affecting the Speaker's duties, that we should bear in mind that the prime requisite of his duties is that he be impartial.
Perhaps the duty of a Speaker has never been better expressed than in the following quotation from Hon. Ernest Lapointe, which is quoted in an article by James H. Aitchison of Dalhousie University entitled "The Speakership of the Canadian House of Commons". He said:
"Impartiality on the part of the Speaker is the supreme law of his office. It is essential that every member should have the conviction that when our colleague ascends the throne of the Speaker he ceases to be the man of the party and becomes the man of the whole house."
That is the end of the quotation from Hon. Ernest Lapointe. Mr. Aitchison continues:
When Lapointe moved the election (for the second time) of Lemieux to the Speaker's chair he formulated in these words the prime requirement of the Speakership of the popular branch of the legislature of a parliamentary democracy patterned on the classical British model.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the Speaker is placed under a duty to abstain from partisan political action not only in fact but to make it apparent to all, and particularly to his fellow members of parliament, that he has no part in party politics. He is in fact like Caesar's wife: Not only must he be pure but he must be above suspicion.
The particular incident from which I understand this amendment arises relates to the activities of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) when he was still occupying the position of Speaker following the election in April 1963. The hon. member made some reference to the fact that at that time he was exercising those duties; he also made some reference to the fact that he was exercising them even though, during the interval after he was elected Speaker of the House, he accepted a position as minister of the crown. So that while he was under the solemn trust to the members of the House of Commons as their Speaker he accepted an appointment as a minister of the outgoing government and participated actively in a

campaign against those members of the House of Commons to whom he owed the duty of impartiality.
The Speaker is in an anomalous position when elections are called because he must be re-elected to the house. However, I would point out that while he may be under an [DOT]obligation to regain election in his own constituency he certainly is under no obligation to carry on an active campaign on behalf of the government in office as a whole.
It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker-and I put it forward respectfully to the house-that this was a serious thrust at a fundamental democratic right in this country. Perhaps criticism of this particular action has not been put better than by a native Albertan, a distinguished academic from the hon. member's own province, Mr. Denis Smith, a former lecturer in political science at York University, now at Trent University, in an article which he wrote appearing in the Canadian Forum for April 1963. He refers in particular to the state of the Speakership at that time and says:
The election of Mr. Michener was auspicious; his unanimous re-election to the chair in the 24th parliament suggested that the prime minister-
The reference in that case is to the hon. member for Prince Albert, the present Leader [DOT]of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
-and the whole membership of the house, had learned the lesson of the pipe line debate. But from then on, while Mr. Michener dignified the Speakership, the prime minister-
Again I would remind the house that that is the Leader of the Opposition.
-progressively allowed political interest to cloud his conception of an independent Speaker. The office of Deputy Speaker was used, as the Speakership had once been used, as a test for prospective ministers. The prime minister did not always defer to the Chair, as parliamentary practice and the prime minister's own conscience should have demanded. Finally, after the defeat of Mr. Michener and the accession to the chair of Mr. Lambert in the last parliament, Mr. Diefenbaker gave up entirely his belief in an independent Speaker. In his desperate search for ministers after the cabinet crisis, he turned to Mr. Lambert, and by implication made the Chair once more a stepping-stone to political office.
We have in question here, Mr. Speaker, not so much the question of whether or not it is desirable for the Clerk of the House to exercise these duties, and my personal opinion is that the present Clerk of this house as an experienced former member of this house is well qualified in the operation of the administrative duties of this house, but the question of conflict of interest which faced
House of Commons Act the hon. member for Edmonton. West when he was in that particular position.
It is my suggestion that the best way in which we can remove that conflict is by taking the responsibility for these administrative duties away from the Speaker when he is in this kind of half life-in the position of perhaps not having been re-elected or, if reelected, not having been selected again as Speaker of the house.
Mr. Speaker, the kind of measure which the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Whelan) has put forward is the kind of measure which should commend itself to the house so that that kind of conflict of interest or breach of the impartiality which is expected of the Speaker will not occur again.
